parameter_units: Native lengths are millimetres unless the command description specifies another unit.

commands.label: Capture Adaptive Context
commands.parameters: {sources:[{id,host:{type:frame,point}|{type:face|edge|vertex,...}}]} ordered project references captured as full world frames, with persistent source identities; a snapshot, not a live constraint

commands.label: Evaluate Adaptive Placement
commands.parameters: {id} evaluate an adaptive component, returning exact local placement, ordered dependencies, valid geometry and diagnostics for replay

commands.label: Move Adaptive Point
commands.parameters: {id, number, to: [x,y,z]} adaptive point `number` of adaptive component `id` moved to project point `to`, its axes kept: what dragging its grip does

commands.label: Place Adaptive Instances
commands.parameters: {family,type?,placements:[{adaptive:{frames,context?,bindings?},at?:[x,y],level?,angle?,offset?,params?}]} batch placement, up to 1000 instances, in one undo step. The frames are the project's (as adaptive_capture gives them): each instance builds on them wherever it stands, holding them in its own axes; `at` defaults to the first frame's point

commands.label: Add Point
commands.parameters: {id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height

commands.label: Add Split Line
commands.parameters: {id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now

commands.label: Align
commands.parameters: {id, reference: [[x,y],[x,y]], line: [[x,y],[x,y]], lock?: true, to?: id} aligns an element's picked line with a reference in plan: turns by the smaller angle about the picked line's midpoint, then moves it onto the reference, keeping its size. Doors and windows slide along their host wall; they cannot turn independently. With `lock`, Revit's padlock: the line and the reference (of element `to`, else whatever has a line along it) are kept on one line after every command, as a locked dimension keeps its length; refused when that can't hold with the other locks. Returns {aligned, angle, by, line} (the picked line where it went), and the lock's id

commands.label: Autosave
commands.parameters: {path, compress?} atomically write a recovery snapshot, keeping the project path and undo history: plain JSON, or zipped with `compress: true`, as `save` writes

commands.label: Check Bathroom Volumes
commands.parameters: {fixture: {outline?: [[x, y], …], shower?: [x, y], floor?, rim?}, things: [{name?, kind, at: [x, y, z], ip?, class?, supply?, voltage?, rcd?, serving?}], public?, standard?} which of the volumes around a bathtub or a shower each thing stands in, and whether it may stand there, as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.1 asks. The numbers are data (`data/bath-volumes.json`, one rule set for each standard, every volume and every thing it allows naming its source): `standard` names the set, `NBR 5410:2004` the default and only one so far. `fixture` is the tub, tray or recess in plan (`outline`, mm) or the outlet of a shower with no tray (`shower`), `floor` the level one stands on (mm, 0 by default) and `rim` the tub's rim above it (mm, 0 by default). Volume 0 is the inside up to the rim (none for a shower with no tray); 1 over it up to 2.25 m (0.6 m round a shower with no tray); 2 out 0.60 m more, up to 3 m, so over volume 1 too; 3 out 2.40 m more, up to 2.25 m. A thing's `kind` is outlet, switch (any device that protects, isolates or controls), box (a junction box; `serving` when it connects only equipment of these volumes), luminaire, heater (a water heater) or equipment; `ip` the second digit of its IP code, `class` I, II or III, `supply` mains (the default), selv (with `voltage`, V) or separation (its own separating transformer), `rcd` the residual-current device that protects it, mA. Each comes back with its `volume` (null outside them all), the least `ip_min` there (IPX7, 4, 3 and 1; IPX5 in volumes 2 and 3 of a `public` bathroom), `allowed`, `ok` (allowed, with an IP known and enough), `why` and `sources`; `failing` names the things that are not `ok`. In volume 0 only SELV up to 12 V; no outlet or switch in volumes 0 to 2 (a switch at SELV excepted); a heater of class I or II in volume 1 and 2, a luminaire of class II in volume 2; an outlet in volume 3 by separation, SELV or a residual-current device of 30 mA at most. The volumes are measured straight: the walls and partitions they go around are not seen (`not_covered`), so what stands behind one is taken as inside. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Beam
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°

commands.label: Cable Tray
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep

commands.label: Cabling
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to

commands.label: CAD Layers
commands.parameters: {id, hide?: [layer, …], show?: [layer, …], view?} a CAD import's layers, each with its colour and linetype and whether it's shown; `hide` and `show` change which it shows in every view, or with `view` in that view only (its Visibility/Graphics, by the drawing's name)

commands.label: Query
commands.parameters: {id, at: [x, y], reach?} what of a CAD import lies nearest `at`, within `reach` mm (100 unless given): its kind, layer, colour, linetype and weight, as Revit's Query

commands.label: Camera
commands.parameters: {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in

commands.label: Ceiling
commands.parameters: {point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it

commands.label: Circuit
commands.parameters: Two commands in one id. (1) A circuit of the model: {devices: [ids], panel: id, name?, number?, rating?, poles?, voltage?, classification?, demand_factor?, wires?} makes one: the devices (components of a family with a power connector, each in one circuit) on a distribution board, behind a breaker of `rating` amperes (a standard one for the load unless given) and `poles` (the devices'), at the `voltage` its board's system supplies (a voltage of the project; unset, the system's line-to-neutral for one pole, line-to-line for more), `number` on the board (the next free unless given), `classification` (its devices'), `demand_factor` (above 0 up to 1, 1) and `wires` {hot: {wire_type, section}, neutral?, ground?} (sections of the wire type's table, in mm²). {id, ...} changes one, merging fields; {id, add?: [ids], remove?: [ids]} its devices; {id, delete: true} takes it away; {list: true} or {panel: id} lists the circuits, all or a board's, each with its devices, installed and demand VA, current and the load of each pole. A device draws at its connector's voltage, within the band of the circuit's voltage, on as many poles as the circuit has, and a refusal names both voltages. Circuits are not copied. (2) The sizing:

commands.label: Column
commands.parameters: {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, attach_top?, attach_base?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level` (`top_offset` mm above it). `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor (id) its top follows from below, or its base stands on, as a wall's do

commands.label: Compare Cross-Check
commands.parameters: {path? | text?} another tool's numbers of the project export_crosscheck described, a table `kind,id,quantity,value` (rooms' enclosed, area_m2, perimeter_m; walls' length_m, openings; floors' area_m2, volume_m3), from the file at `path` or `text`, held against the project's own: how many were `compared`, those that `differ` (ours and theirs), and those `only_ours` and `only_theirs`, the first 100 of each with their counts

commands.label: Component
commands.parameters: {family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}, adaptive?: {frames: {number: {origin,x,y,z}}, context?}, host?: {level: name|id} | {plane: name|id|GUID} | {face: {element: id|GUID, face: exterior|interior|top|bottom}}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level (none: its family's Default Elevation, unless work plane-based), and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's). A work plane-based family may go on a reference plane (`host` `plane`, Place on Work Plane): `at` [x, y] is taken straight onto the plane, [x, y, z] along its normal (an upright plane needs it), `offset` is its Offset from Host along the normal, `level` its Schedule Level (by default the highest level at or below it); it follows the plane when the plane moves, upright or, its family not Always Vertical, tilted with the plane (a plane turned about the vertical turns it too). Or on a face (Place on Face): a wall's `exterior` or `interior` side, `at` [x, y, z] taken to its nearest point there; a floor's, a ceiling's or a roof's `top` or `bottom`, `at` [x, y] taken straight onto it (a roof's slope or a shaped floor's plane under it); it follows the face when its host moves, turns, or changes slope, thickness or type, goes with a floor, a ceiling or a roof moved or copied, and is deleted with its host; one its face no longer reaches stays on the face's plane, with a warning. Always Vertical keeps it plumb on every face; else it stands out along the face's normal (hanging from an underside), and on a wall's side `angle` turns it from the face's level direction, so it turns with the wall. An adaptive family's component is placed by its points (`adaptive`, else the family's test placement) and takes no `host` plane

commands.label: Conduit
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

commands.label: Conduit Fill
commands.parameters: {section, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, circuits?, reduced_neutral?, family?, size?} the fill of a conduit as NBR 5410 asks, for the conductors of a circuit (its phases, neutral and protective conductor, of `section` mm²) times `circuits` in the same conduit (1): their cross-sections by outside diameter over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. `family` (pvc-thread, pvc-solder, steel-heavy, steel-rir; pvc-thread) and `size` (its mark, e.g. 3/4"; none: the smallest that fits). The dimensions are the makers' own from their catalogues, each family naming maker, document, page and address; the inside diameter is the outside less twice the wall. The data covers the flexible 750 V PVC cable of 0.5 to 240 mm² only: there is no `insulation` key, and a section above 240 mm² is `pending`, never guessed. `sections_mm2` lists the conductors of one circuit (`circuits` of them are in the conduit). Cable trays are not sized. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Convert Coordinates
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y,z], …], from: internal|base|shared|wgs84, to: internal|base|shared|wgs84, location?} each point from one frame to another, mm: `internal`, the file's own, where geometry is; `base`, from the Project Base Point; `shared`, the map coordinates of the active site (or of the site `location` names); `wgs84`, [longitude, latitude, elevation mm], through the site's map system (its `crs`, a projected EPSG code). Returns points

commands.label: Convert Spline
commands.parameters: {id} a detail line that is a spline through points becomes the same curve by its control points, exactly; one by its control points becomes a spline through points within 0.05 mm of it

commands.label: Coordinates
commands.parameters: {base?: [x,y,z], survey?: [x,y,z], move?: point|system, acquire?: link or CAD id, reset?: true} the project's coordinates. `reset` puts the active location back on the internal origin (shared coordinates the file's own) and both points on it, and pins every link placed by base points or shared coordinates by hand where it stands, so none moves. `acquire` takes the shared coordinates of a link (its id; a BIMCraft project or an IFC file) or of a CAD drawing placed in the project (its coordinates taken for the map's) where it stands now, as Revit's Acquire Coordinates: this project's active location is solved so that the link's origin has the link's map coordinates here and its true north agrees. Without parameters, reports them: the internal origin, the Project Base Point and the Survey Point, each `internal` (the file's own mm, where geometry is) and `shared` (the active location's map coordinates, mm), the `active` location and every location. `base` moves the Project Base Point, the reference elevations and spot coordinates measure from; it moves no geometry. `survey` moves the Survey Point: `move: point` (the default) moves it alone, so the building stays where it is in the world and the point's shared coordinates change; `move: system` carries the shared system with it, so it keeps its shared coordinates and the building moves in the world

commands.label: Copy
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

commands.label: Trim/Extend to Corner
commands.parameters: {ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep

commands.label: Create Group
commands.parameters: {ids, name?} a detail group made of detail lines, filled regions and text notes of one view, as Revit's Create Group: they become type `name`'s members (Group 1, 2… unless told), and one group of it takes their place, its origin the middle of them. Place it again with detail_group; ungroup gives its members back. Returns {id, name}

commands.label: Crop View
commands.parameters: {view, region?: [[x, y], [x, y]] | null} crops a level's plan to the region's south-west and north-east corners (plan mm), or a section or an elevation to its bottom left and top right (along its line from its start, and up: its line then runs between them, and the notes in it stay put); null uncrops it; without a region, it crops to what the view shows now

commands.label: Delete
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…], keep_finishes?} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted. A room takes the floor and the ceiling connected to it (see `room_finish`), unless `keep_finishes`: then they stay, as ordinary ones

commands.label: Delete Type
commands.parameters: {category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type?} deletes a type of a category (`category` and `type`), a family (`family`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`), as Revit's Delete on one in the Project Browser does; refused while an element uses it (it says how many), and for the last type of a category or of a family

commands.label: Demand and Service Category
commands.parameters: {utility: CPFL|ENEL|CELESC, building?: residential|other, system?: 127/220|220/380, area?, outlets?, lighting_points?, lighting_outlets?: {use, kw, pf?}, heaters?, boilers?, appliances?, stoves?: [{w, count?}], air_conditioners?: [{btu | va and w, count?}], air_use?: residential|commercial, motors?: [{cv, phases: 1|3 | kva and kw, count?}], special?: [{kind: arc_weld|resistance_weld|xray, kw, count?}], hydromassage?: [{w, count?}]} the demand D (kVA) of an installation and the category of service it asks of the `utility`, by that utility's own standard, since NBR 5410 gives no demand factors. `utility` is required: CPFL (GED 13 version 2.24, 18/09/2020: CPFL Paulista, Piratininga, Santa Cruz and RGE) or ENEL (ET 1569 version 01, 29/01/2024) or CELESC (N-321.0001, revision of December 2025); any other is refused until its tables are added. CELESC, too, leaves the demand to the designer: `{utility: CELESC, network?: 220/380|220/440, installed_kw, phases?: 1|2|3, demand_kva?}` gives the category of Tabela 01 by the installed load (A single-phase 220 V, M single-phase 220/440 V, B two-phase, C three-phase), its breaker, phases and wires, the connection and entry branches and the earthing conductor; `phases` picks the supply an appliance asks for whatever the load. ENEL does not work out a demand, for its specification leaves it to the designer (item 7.7.2): `{utility: ENEL, network: aerial|aerial_120_240|underground|underground_submersible, installed_kw, phases?: 1|2|3, demand_kva?}` frames the supply by the installed load in kW: Anexo A (aerial, 127/220 V), C (aerial, 120/240 V), D (underground, surface, 127/220 V) or E (underground, submersible): the category, the power it makes available (E prints none and gives the junction box), the breaker, the connection and entry branches, the earthing conductor and the measurement; where two categories hold the load (B2 and C1 of A) `candidates` names both and `phases` picks one. `network: aerial_delta` (Anexo B, 120/240 V delta with a neutral) goes by `demand_current_a`, the designer's demand current in A, and gives the smallest breaker that holds it. `demand_kva` is carried as the designer gives it. For CPFL: `D = a + b + c + d + e + f + g + h + i`: a lighting and outlets (in a dwelling, `area` m² gives the least outlets of Tabela 2, or `outlets` above 250 m² (100 W each, and the kitchen's 3 of 600 W), and `lighting_points` of 100 W; in another building `lighting_outlets` declares its `use` (auditorium, shop, barbershop, club, school, office, garage, hospital, hotel, church, industry, restaurant), kW and power factor, by Tabela 18), b `heaters` (showers, taps, instant heaters, irons: Tabela 4 by their number in all), c `boilers` (Tabela 5), d `appliances` (dryers, ovens, dishwashers, microwaves: Tabela 6), e `stoves` (Tabela 7), f `air_conditioners` (a `btu` of Tabela 8, or `va` and `w`; a factor of 1, or Tabela 9 for `air_use` commercial), g `motors` (a `cv` of Tabela 14 or 15 with its `phases`, or `kva` and `kw`; Tabela 10 by rank, the biggest first), h `special` equipment (Tabela 11, power factor 0.75), i `hydromassage` (Tabela 10). `w` is the power of one appliance in watts. It replies the installed load (kW), each term, D, and the `category` of Tabela 1A (`system` 127/220, the default) or 1B (220/380) with its breaker, cable, conduit and earthing conductor: by the installed load up to 25 kW, by D above, `null` where the table ends (75 kW; D of 76 or 82 kVA). Not covered: the other columns of Tabela 1, the cables of Tabelas 1D and 1E, and the starting of motors (Tabela 13) (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Demand Factors
commands.parameters: {class?, factor?, delete?: true} the project's demand factors by classification: the share (above 0 up to 1) of the load of the circuits of a `class` (lighting, receptacle…, as their devices' connectors name it) that counts in a board's demand load and its panel schedule, on top of each circuit's own `demand_factor`. A class with none counts whole. Without `class`, lists them

commands.label: Detail Level
commands.parameters: {view, detail?: coarse | medium | fine} how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts: coarse, one poché and openings as their gaps; medium, compound layers with the lines between them and an opening's leaf, swing and glass; fine (the default), the layers' patterns and a floor's surface pattern too. A family's forms and symbols with Visibility Settings (`family` `visibility`) are drawn only at the levels they tick, in every view. A 3D view (`{3D}` for the default one, made when its level first changes) has a detail level too, which only those settings read. Without `detail` it only says what the view has

commands.label: Place Detail Group
commands.parameters: {type, at: [x,y], angle?, mirrored?, view?} a detail group of type `type` placed in a view (the lowest plan by default): its members drawn with their origin at `at`, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, mirrored across their x axis first when `mirrored`. Move, copy, rotate and mirror take it whole

commands.label: Detail Line
commands.parameters: {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

commands.label: Parameter Dictionary
commands.parameters: {path, name?, version?, add?: [{name, kind?, description?, group?, categories?, guid?, read_only?, scope?: instance|type}], names?: [project parameters], merge?: [paths], remove?: [names or GUIDs], skip_conflicts?: true} makes or changes the dictionary file at `path` (.bimparams); the project isn't changed. A definition with a GUID the file has replaces it; a new one gets a GUID; another GUID under a name the file has stops it unless `skip_conflicts`. `merge` takes in other files of any kind `parameter_import` reads. A change counts up its `revision` and dates it `changed`. `version` is a label of the team's own. Answers what the file now holds

commands.label: Load Parameter Dictionary
commands.parameters: {path} or {name, remove: true}: a dictionary's file loaded in the project, which remembers it and saves it as part of the project; several can be. Nothing comes into the project until `parameter_import`. A dictionary moved is found by its GUID, and takes its new path; another dictionary of a name already loaded is refused. `remove` is refused while a parameter comes from it

commands.label: Aligned Dimension
commands.parameters: {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. With `id`, it edits that dimension instead: `refs` replaces them (two at least, no duplicates; its locks and segment texts follow the pairs of references they were on, and those of a pair gone are dropped), `at`, `kind`, `orient`, `type`, its text and `equality` change when given; a dimension Align locked can't be edited until its lock is taken off. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a column's or structural column's centre line along its angle (the default; west to east at angle 0), `across`, its centre line square to that (south to north), its left or right face (of its angle's direction: north or south), or its start or end cap (west or east); a round column has only its two centre lines (radial: its edge); a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a column's corner or centre line's end, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm, found in the plan of `level` as it draws it: among the walls and columns its cut plane passes through, whatever level they stand on (a column from a level below that runs up through it too), their doors and windows, the grids and the plan's detail lines. It follows what it measures

commands.label: Aligned Dimension in 3D
commands.parameters: {refs: [ref, ref], at: [x, y, z], view?, type?} an aligned dimension in a 3D view (the default 3D view unless `view` names another, by name or id), kept by the view and drawn in it and on a sheet that holds it: how far apart its two references are, along a line through `at` moved square off them. A ref is {at: [x, y, z]}, a point of the model, or {at, edge: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]]}, a point on an edge, which it measures square to (from a point, to the edge's line; between two parallel edges, how far apart they are). `type` is a dimension type, the aligned one's unless told. On the desktop, Aligned Dimension (DI) in the 3D view runs it. Returns its id and its length

commands.label: Dimension Constraints
commands.parameters: {id, equal?: bool, locked?: [segment, …]} an aligned or linear dimension's constraints, as Revit's EQ and padlocks: `equal` keeps its segments equal (what it measures to between its first and last moves to keep them so, its ends staying); `locked` lists the segments (counted from 0, west to east or south to north) kept at the lengths they have now. After any command, what a constrained dimension measures to moves with what the command moved, or the command is refused, saying which dimension can't be kept

commands.label: Delete Dimension Segment
commands.parameters: {id, segment} takes one segment out of an aligned or a linear dimension's chain: the chains either side of it stay, each measured to the references it had, so the deleted segment's measures are not made one with a neighbour; the left chain keeps this dimension, the right one is new at the same line. A chain left with one segment loses its equality, and a chain's only segment takes the dimension away. Locks and segment texts follow the references that remain. Returns {id, deleted, values, right?, right_values?}, or {deleted: id}

commands.label: Dimension Text
commands.parameters: {id, segment?, prefix?, suffix?, above?, below?, replace?} a dimension's text, as Revit's Dimension Text: what goes before and after its numbers, over and under them, or in place of them. With `segment` (its numbers counted from 0, west to east or south to north, as `labels` lists them), that one's own, over the dimension's where it says something; an empty text clears it, and a segment with none left goes back to the dimension's

commands.label: Dimension Types
commands.parameters: {name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, …values} a dimension type of the project's, as Revit's type parameters, lengths mm on paper. Graphics: `string` continuous|baseline|ordinate (Dimension String Type; baseline lines `baseline_spacing` apart, 7), `tick` diagonal|arrow|open_arrow|dot|none, `tick_size` (2), `line_pen` and `tick_pen` (0 to 16; 4 and 7), `color` ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b]), `line_extension` past the outer witness lines (0.8), `witness` gap_to_element|fixed (Witness Line Control), `witness_length` when fixed (5), `witness_gap` off what it measures (0.6), `witness_extension` past the dimension line (0.8), `centre_mark` on radial and diameter ones. Text: `font` (as text types take; Arial), `text_size` (2.5), `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor` (1), `text_offset` off the line (1), `background` opaque|transparent, `read` up_then_left|up_then_right (Read Convention), `units` (mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in; null for the project's) and `decimals` (0 to 6; null as the units show), `radius_symbol` (R), `diameter_symbol` (Ø), `equality_text` (EQ). A new one starts as `like` says, else as the default. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial` (aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in it) and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial` (radial and diameter ones). `rename` renames it, its dimensions following; `delete` takes it away while no dimension is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

commands.label: Dimension Value
commands.parameters: {id, value, segment?, hold?: start|end|both|ref} types a length into an aligned or a linear dimension's segment (the first unless told), as a click on its number does: with `hold` `start` (the default), the segment's first reference stays and its second moves along the dimension so the segment is `value` mm; with `end`, the second stays and the first moves; with a reference {id, face?, point?}, that one stays and the other moves; a locked segment is locked at it, and the other locks hold, or it is refused. For an equal dimension, `start` and `end` name its own first and last reference, and every segment becomes `value` (the far end moves); `both` keeps both ends and takes only the value they already divide into evenly. One wall's own length (its two ends) resizes it: both ends free or both joined move evenly, one joined moves its free end; its thickness, a door's or window's width and a column's size are their type's and are refused. Returns {id, moved, by, values}

commands.label: Distribution Systems
commands.parameters: {name?, phases?: 1|2|3, wires?, l_l?, l_n?, l_g?, ground?, rename?, delete?: true} a distribution system of the project's electrical settings. `wires` counts the line conductors and the neutral, not the protective one (3 phases: 3 or 4). `l_l`, `l_n` and `l_g` name the voltages between two lines, a line and the neutral, and a line and earth (at least one; `l_l` from 2 phases; with 3 phases `l_l` is about 1.73 times `l_n`), each a `voltage` of the project; "" takes one away. `ground` is the earthing: TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT or IT. A voltage the project lacks is refused, and the refusal lists the ones it has. Without `name`, lists them

commands.label: Door
commands.parameters: {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; without `level`, prefer the lowest level at or above elevation 0 whose plan cuts a wall there, then the highest below 0; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door; an explicit `level` different from the wall's places it at that level's elevation, otherwise at the wall's base; it may rise past a low wall's top, as Revit lets it

commands.label: Dormer
commands.parameters: {host, at: [x, y], width?, height?, slope?, window?, type?} a dormer on roof `host`, its front wall across the slope through `at`: walls of `type` `width` mm (1600) apart, standing on the roof and `height` mm (1200) tall at the front, under a gable roof of its own sloping `slope` degrees (30) that runs back into the host; the host open under it, and with `window` (a window type) a window in its front. Replies with its roof, walls and window

commands.label: Down Conductor
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to

commands.label: Check Surge Protection
commands.parameters: {region: AQ1|AQ2|AQ3, overhead?, accepted_risk?, risk_to_people?, purpose?: line|direct|both, earthing?: TT|TN-S|TN-C|IT, uo?, before_dr?, system?: 120/208|127/220|220/380|230/400|277/480|400/690, neutral?, phases?: 1|3, existing?, signal_lines?: [telephone|data|video|tv|antenna|interconnection]} surge protection (DPS) of a power line as NBR 5410:2004 asks. It is required where the line is `overhead` (wholly or partly, or the installation has an overhead line itself) and the `region` is AQ2 (more than 25 days of thunderstorms a year), or in any AQ3 region (5.4.2.1.1); `accepted_risk` is the project taking a calculated risk the standard allows, never where the omission may put people at risk (`risk_to_people`), and `exempt` says it was taken. When it is required the reply gives where it stands by its `purpose` (line, the default: surges the line carries and switching surges, at the entry or the main board; direct: lightning on the building, at the entry; both; `existing` adds the meter box of an existing individual unit), with `earthing` (and whether the line has a `neutral`, yes by default) the connection scheme or schemes of Figure 13, with `phases` (3 by default) the least nominal discharge current (5 kA for each mode; 20 kA three-phase or 10 kA single-phase between the neutral and the PE of scheme 3) and impulse current (12.5 kA; 50 or 25 kA there), and the connecting conductors (4 mm² copper at least, 16 mm² against direct lightning, 0.5 m in all). With `earthing`, `uc_min` is the least continuous operating voltage Uc of Tabela 49 for each pair of points the device connects (1.1 Uo; Uo between the neutral and the PE; √3 Uo phase to PE in IT; U in IT without a neutral), in volts when `uo`, the phase-to-neutral voltage, is given. `signal_lines` are the external signal lines, each protected at the entry. Not covered: the overcurrent device of the DPS (6.3.5.2.5) and coordination (`not_covered`). `before_dr` is for a DPS upstream of a DR, which in TT takes scheme 3 only (6.3.5.2.6 b); with `earthing` the reply also gives the follow current between neutral and PE and the short-circuit the DPS must withstand (6.3.5.2.4 e). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Check Residual-Current Protection
commands.parameters: {circuits: [{name, points: [{place, kind, rating?, height?, outdoor?}], residual?, it_continuity?}], building?: residential|other, standard?} which circuits NBR 5410:2004 asks additional protection by a high-sensitivity residual-current device (DR, 30 mA at most) for. The rules are data (`data/dr-check.json`, one rule set for each standard, every rule naming its source): `standard` names the set, `NBR 5410:2004` the default and only one so far, and the answer gives `standard`, `standard_source` and, for each circuit, the `sources` of its `reasons`. A circuit's `points` are what it serves: `place` is bath (a place with a bathtub or a shower), external, kitchen (or pantry-kitchen), laundry, service (service area), garage, wet (another wet internal area) or dry; `kind` is outlet, lighting or fixed (another point of use); `rating` an outlet's rated current in A (32 A at most is covered; unknown, it is taken as covered), `height` a light's in mm (in a dwelling a light 2500 mm up or more in the wet rooms is left out), `outdoor` an internal outlet that may feed equipment outdoors. It is needed where any point is in a bath place, an outlet is in an external area or may feed equipment outdoors, and, in a dwelling (the default `building`), any point is in a kitchen, laundry, service area, garage or wet internal area (outside a dwelling, only their outlets). `it_continuity` marks an IT circuit that must not be cut, for the safety of persons or to keep lives, which is left out (`exempt`). `residual` is the rated residual current of the device the circuit has, in mA: `ok` is whether it is 30 or less, and `missing` names the circuits that need one and have none. Not covered: the further rules for the volumes of a bathroom and for swimming pools (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Size a Sanitary Drain
commands.parameters: {units?, fixtures?: {wc?, lav?, sink?, shower?, laundry?}, role?: branch|main|stack, slope?, floors?, min_dn?} the DN of a sanitary drain as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) it carries: `units`, or `fixtures` counted (Tabela 3: a water closet 6 UHC and DN 100, a lavatory 1 and 40, a sink 3 and 50, a shower 2 and 40, a laundry tub 3 and 40; the drain is never smaller than the fixtures' own). `role`: a `branch` (ramal de esgoto, Tabela 5, the default), a `main` (subcoletor or coletor predial, Tabela 7 by `slope`, a fraction, 0.01 by default; DN 100 at least) or a `stack` (tubo de queda, Tabela 6 by the building's `floors`, up to three or more). `min_dn` is the largest drain flowing into it. Replies with the `dn`, what it carries (`capacity`) and the `minimum_dn` the fixtures ask. A blank in the standard's table means not allowed: DN 100 and 150 carry nothing in a building drain at 0.5 %, and a branch or a building drain never borrows the other's table. For a `main` every fixture given counts, where item 5.1.4.2 counts only the largest fixture of each bathroom in a residential building: pass `units` already reduced to follow it. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Duct
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")

commands.label: Duplicate View
commands.parameters: {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

commands.label: Edit Boundary
commands.parameters: {id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The outline must be simple, as `floor` says; a line that crosses itself is found as two that cross are

commands.label: Modify Sub Elements
commands.parameters: {id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height the top has there. Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)

commands.label: Edit Work Plane
commands.parameters: {ids, host: {level: name|id} | {plane: name|id|GUID} | {face: {element: id|GUID, face}}} puts components on a level (at their plan point, on it), a reference plane of the project or a face of a wall, a floor, a ceiling or a roof (taken onto it; one from another plane or face keeps its Offset from Host). {family, form | ref_line: id|GUID, host: {plane: name|id|GUID} | {line, face} | a name as the Work Plane dialog lists it (`Reference Line 1 : Vertical`), keep?, dry_run?} puts a family's form or reference line on another of its planes: it moves with the plane, as Revit's Edit Work Plane, keeping its profile and start and end in the new plane's axes; with `keep` it stays where it is, which only a plane parallel to its old one allows (a reference line, only one it already lies on)

commands.label: Elements
commands.parameters: {category?, level?, field?, value?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…; a component's `room`, the GUID of the room its family's room calculation point, else its insertion point, is in); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do. `field` is one its category's schedule has (`Type`, `Mark`, a project parameter), and `value` what it holds: text in any case, a number (mm, m² for an area), yes or no, or `""` for text holding none; without `value`, those holding one (a yes or no reads no when unset)

commands.label: Elevation
commands.parameters: {on?: id, reference?: [[x,y],[x,y]], facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view. With `on` (a wall, a line, a floor's, roof's or ceiling's edge, a grid or any element with a straight edge, the project's or a link's by the id its view gives it) and `at`, it looks square at that element's straight edge nearest `at` (a wall's centre line) from `at`'s side of it: its mark stands at `at`, or 1.5 m out from the edge when `at` is on it (within a metre). `reference` gives the line itself instead of `on`. That line is kept in the elevation as `reference`, a line of its own and no tie to the element: moved to the line's other side the elevation turns round to look at it still, and `modify` with `reference` null lets it go. Without those, of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

commands.label: Explode Polyline
commands.parameters: {id} takes a detail line that is a polyline apart into a line or an arc for each segment, in its view and style; the first keeps its id. Revit has no shortcut for it: EX is ours, PX being the Plumbing Fixture's on the desktop

commands.label: Export
commands.parameters: {format, view?, views?, print_set?, path?, folder?, name?, folders?: flat|by_format, combine?, overwrite?: false, page?, quality?, ifc_origin?, selected?, pdf?} writes views, sheets, schedules or the project out as `format` (an id or an extension from `export_formats`: pdf, svg, png, ifc4, glb, csv, xlsx…). `view` (or a list, `views`) is an element's id or GUID, a view's name or a sheet's number; none or `project` is the whole project (model formats only); `print_set` names a set's views and sheets (`print_set`). `path` writes one file there (several views to a PDF go in it as pages); or `folder` takes a file each, named by the `name` template (`{SheetNumber} - {SheetName}`, `{ViewName}`, `{ProjectName}`, `{ViewType}`, `{Level}`, `{Scale}`, `{Format}`, `{Date}`, `{Time}`; `/` makes folders), numbered rather than written over unless `overwrite`; `combine` names the one file each format that holds pages puts them all in. `page`: {paper?: A3|ARCH D|Letter…, size?: [w,h] mm, orientation?: auto|landscape|portrait, margin?: mm, scale?: original|fit|{custom: n}, anchor?: centre|top_left…, colour?: colour|grey|black, hairlines?, dpi?: 150, region?: [x1, y1, x2, y2] (only what lies inside: a plan's model mm, a sheet's paper mm; every drawing format), pages?: [first, last] or "1, 3, 5-7"}. `pdf`: {archive?: none|a1b|a2b|a2u|a3b|a4 (PDF/A, checked as it is written: a file that wouldn't be one isn't written), version?: "1.4" to "2.0" (1.7), raster? (each page a picture at `page.dpi`), cut_marks? (the pages of a tiled drawing get hairlines in the margin where they meet), title?, author?, subject?, keywords?: [..]}. `ifc_origin` is IFC's, as `save` takes it; `selected` (ids or GUIDs) the elements a BCF topic is about. Returns `written` ({path, format, of}) and `failed` ({of, format, error})

commands.label: Export Cross-Check
commands.parameters: {path?} the project's levels, walls (by their centre lines), floors, shafts, doors, windows and rooms as plain numbers in mm, which tools/revit-crosscheck builds again in another BIM tool to hold its numbers against ours (compare_crosscheck): written to `path`, or returned as `description` without it

commands.label: Export Fill Patterns
commands.parameters: {path?, names?: [name, …]} the project's fill patterns (those `names` says, else all but the solid ones, which a PAT file can't hold) as a PAT file in mm, written to `path`, or returned as `text` without it

commands.label: Export Formats
commands.parameters: {} the formats `export` writes: each one's `id`, `label`, `extension`, `family`, `status` (stable, experimental or planned: listed, not written yet), what it `takes` (drawing, table, model), whether it `combines` sources in one file and lays drawings on pages (`paged`); and the `tokens` a file name template may hold

commands.label: Falls
commands.parameters: {id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain

commands.label: Load Family
commands.parameters: {name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|integer|angle|area|volume|yesno|material|text|url|familytype, instance?, value?, formula?, group?: constraints|construction|dimensions|graphics|identity-data|materials-and-finishes|text|visibility|electrical|mechanical|plumbing|structural|data|other, shared?: guid, reporting?, of?: category}], parameter?: {name, rename?, …a parameter's fields}, delete_parameter?: [name, …], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{host?: {plane: guid} | {line: guid, face: horizontal|vertical|start|end}, plane?: xy|xz|yz, sketch?: [{start: [a, b], end: [a, b], turn?, axis?} | {centre: [a, b], radius}, …], profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, visibility?, void?, top?: [sketch lines] (a Blend: `sketch` its base at `from`, `top` its top at `to`, each one closed loop in the host plane's axes), sweep?: {profile: [sketch lines], end?: [sketch lines]} (a Sweep: `sketch` is its path, a chain of lines and arcs, open or closed, or one circle, and `profile` its profile drawn square to the path, x to the right looking along it and y the host's normal; with `end`, a Swept Blend: a path of one line or arc, `profile` at its start and `end` at its end, one loop each), twist?: n (a Blend's top or a Swept Blend's end profile paired from its vertex n on: Edit Vertices' Twist)}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?, visibility?: {coarse?, medium?, fine?}}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], ref_planes?: [{guid?, name?, start: [x, y, z], end: [x, y, z], up: [x, y, z], reference?: not_a_reference|strong|weak|left|center_left_right|right|front|center_front_back|back|bottom|center_elevation|top, defines_origin?, subcategory?}], ref_plane?: {id | guid, …a plane's fields}, delete_ref_plane?: [id | guid, …], ref_lines?: [{guid?, start: [x, y, z], end: [x, y, z], host?: {plane: guid} | {line: guid, face}, reference?, subcategory?}], ref_line?: {id | guid, …}, delete_ref_line?: [id | guid, …], dimensions?: [{guid?, view?: plan|ceiling|front|back|left|right, refs: [{plane: guid} | {form: guid, end: start|end} | {form: guid, line: guid} | {form: guid, line: guid, point: start|end|centre} | {line: guid, face: horizontal|vertical|start|end}, …], at: [x, y, z], kind?: aligned|radial|diameter, label?: parameter, locked?: [{segment, length}], equal?, alignment?}], dimension?: {id | guid, …a dimension's fields} (none: one added), delete_dimension?: [id | guid, …], invalid_dimensions?: delete, solve?: type, operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed|sectional|roller (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), ifc?: {class, predefined?, object_type?} | null (the IFC class a generic family's components go out as, which one opened from IFC remembers: `IFCPLATE`, `CURTAIN_PANEL`; one IFC4 lacks goes out as a proxy that names it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch|pipe|data|earthing, name?, system?: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, domain?: cold|hot|waste|vent|storm|gas, flow?: in|out|both, at?: [x, y, z], direction?: [x, y, z], size?, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], adaptive?: {nodes, preview?} | null, options?: {work_plane_based?, always_vertical?, cut_with_voids_when_loaded?, shared?, room_calculation_point?: [x, y, z] | null, cut_in_views?: true|false|null, omniclass?: {number, title?} | null} (Revit's Family Category and Parameters: each given merged over what it has, `null` back to its default; `room_calculation_point` is a point in its own axes, mm, numbers or formulas over its length parameters, whose room a component is in (else its insertion point's: `elements` says `room`, IFC references it in that space beside its storey); `cut_in_views` overrides whether sections cut its forms, which by default its category says; `omniclass` is a number of digits and dots (`23.30.20.17`) and a title, which IFC writes as a classification reference on its type; work_plane_based (off), always_vertical (on) and cut_with_voids_when_loaded (off) are kept for later and change nothing yet; shared (off) makes it a shared nested family (below); a reply's `options` has them all), rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, definition?, save?, overwrite?: no|version|version_and_values, shared_nested?: {name: project|family}, nest?: {path | definition, name?, overwrite?, shared_nested?}, nested?: [{name, family}], delete_nested?: [names], nested_instances?: [...], nested_instance?: {id | guid?, family, type, host?, at?: [x, y], offset?, angle?, visible?, visibility?, params?: {name: number | formula}}, delete_nested_instance?: [ids or GUIDs]} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .bimf file (or the .json of earlier versions) at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. `visibility` is Revit's Visibility Settings, drawing only (IFC, schedules and `visible` are untouched; it ANDs with `visible`): {plan?, front_back?, left_right?, coarse?, medium?, fine?, only_when_cut?}, each true by default but `only_when_cut`; `plan` is plans and ceiling plans, cut or not; `front_back` sections and elevations looking along the family's y axis, `left_right` along its x (the nearer axis); a 3D view reads only the detail levels; `only_when_cut` draws it only where a plan's cut plane or a section's line passes through it. A symbol takes only the detail levels (none: medium and fine), and a nested instance's are ANDed with its family's own. A void keeps cutting whatever they say. A door's leaf `{plan: false}` with a symbolic swing shows the swing in plan in place of the leaf. A form patch merges `visibility` whole (`null` takes it away). `parameter` edits the one parameter named (or adds it), as Revit's Edit Parameter: its fields merged over it (`null` takes one away), `rename` keeping its GUID with every formula, form, label and component value following it, and `instance` switched with what its types and components hold moved onto them, not lost (to instance, each component takes its type's value; to type, each type takes what its components agree on, refused where they don't). `delete_parameter` takes parameters away, with their values, refused while a formula, form or label names one. A parameter's `kind`: lengths in mm, areas in mm² and volumes in mm³ (schedules and labels show m² and m³), an `integer` whole (its formula rounds), `text` and `url` words that no formula reads or works out, `familytype` a type of a family of category `of`, for nested families, holding no value yet. `group` is the heading it is listed under (by default its kind's: Dimensions for lengths, areas, volumes and angles, Materials and Finishes for materials, else Other). `shared` makes it a shared parameter, by a GUID that is one name and one kind across the project's families (its name and kind can't change while shared); without it, it is the family's own. `reporting`, a length or an angle, reads a dimension and drives none: no formula, type or component sets it: a dimension labelled with it measures it, and formulas read what it measures (no label may be worked out from one). `dimensions` are Revit's family dimensions (F7): each between two or more parallel references (its planes, the datums, an extrusion's `start` or `end` face, a straight line of a form's sketch, `{form, line}`: the plane through it square to the form's plane, a reference line's face), in order along the way it measures, drawn in `view` (which must see them edge on) with its line through `at`; a line's end or a circle's centre (`point`) is measured along the others. A `radial` or `diameter` one measures one circle of a sketch, seen flat in its view. A line or a form is named by its GUID or its id. A `label` (one segment, a length parameter) makes the segment that parameter's value in every type; `locked` keeps a segment at a length (a labelled one's lock stops dragging from changing it); `equal` keeps its segments equal (EQ); `alignment` is Align's lock, two references, its segment locked at 0. Flexing a type solves them: the planes, extrusion ends and sketch points they measure to take the least change from where they are drawn that holds them all (a datum or a plane that defines the origin stays; a sketch's lines that meet stay joined), and what is drawn on a plane moves with it; a constraint that adds nothing to the others is refused as over-constrained, naming them, and a labelled length of 0 or less is refused for its type. Deleting a plane, a form or a sketch line (a form given again without it) takes it out of the dimensions measuring to it (a dimension left with one reference goes: `deleted_dimensions`). A dimension measuring to what the family hasn't is refused, unless `invalid_dimensions` is `delete` (a reload's Delete Dimension(s)); a file opened leaves it out. `solve` reads, for a type, where its planes, forms' ends and sketches' lines go and each dimension's lengths, and changes nothing. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). `definition` is a family as such a file holds it, given in place of `path` and loaded as the file would be (read strictly). On `path` or `definition`, `overwrite` chooses `no` (keep the project family), `version` (replace the definition, retaining compatible values) or `version_and_values` (also use incoming values). Omitted: legacy merge. Project-only types and instance overrides stay; incoming formulas replace the old ones. Nested families (T6a): `nest` loads a family (a file or a definition) into this one, carried whole inside it; one it nests already defined otherwise is refused unless `overwrite` says version or version_and_values. A nested instance places one of its types on a plane of this family (`host`, by GUID or by name as the Work Plane dialog names it; Ref. Level when none) at `at` in that plane's axes, `offset` along its normal and turned `angle` degrees about it; `params` sets its parameters by numbers or formulas over this family's (Associate Family Parameter: `{"W": "Width"}`; a material or text parameter names one of this family's of its kind, or holds the words), and its geometry is built into this family's own (plans, 3D, IFC). No family nests itself, at any depth; nesting stops at 5 levels, 32 families, 256 instances. A nested family whose option `shared` is on is loaded into the project with the family that nests it: one the project has otherwise is kept (`shared_nested`: project, the default) or overwritten (`family`); a dry run lists them in `shared_conflicts`, and one shared family is one definition across the project's families. Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base): each is drawn on its `host`, a plane of the family, in that plane's own axes, and swept along its normal from `from` to `to`. Every family has three datums, pinned, with the same GUIDs in every family: Ref. Level (9e3c0a10-1f0b-4d8c-8a5e-0000000000a1, its xy, normal +z), Center (Front/Back) (…00a2, its xz: x along +x, y up, normal -y) and Center (Left/Right) (…00a3, its yz: x along +y, y up, normal +x); no host is Ref. Level. `plane` is the old shorthand for them, read as it always was: `xy` up, `xz` along +y (stored on Center (Front/Back) with `from` and `to` negated), `yz` along x. `ref_planes` adds planes of its own: the line `start` to `end` it is drawn as and `up`, its other direction (normal (end - start) × up; its axes x along the line, y up made square to it, its origin the point of it nearest the family's origin); names are unique, each of left through top is one plane's or line's, and `defines_origin` (one plane square to each of x, y and z; the datums until another takes it) is kept but doesn't move the origin yet. `ref_lines` are reference lines drawn on a `host` (lying on it), each with four planes a form may be drawn on: `horizontal` (its host's, through it), `vertical` (square to that through it), `start` and `end` (square to it at each end), their origin its start (`end`'s its end). A line or a plane may carry a `pivot` (F7d; `ref_line`/`ref_plane` patch it, `null` takes it off): it keeps one point of it (`at`: `start`, `end` or `{"along": mm}`, a plane's along the line it is drawn as) on a point (`to`: `{"planes": [g, g]}` where two planes holding its axis cross, `{"line": g, "point": "start"|"end"}`, `{"form": g, "line": g, "point": …}` a sketch's point, or `{"fixed": [x, y, z]}`) and turns about it, its axis the normal of what a line is drawn on, a plane's `up`; its swing, degrees counter-clockwise from `from` (`drawn`, the default, `{"plane": g}` or `{"line": g}`), is the Angle parameter `parameter`, else its own `angle` (which an angular dimension may set instead), within `min` and `max` if given (a value past them is refused, naming them). What is drawn on a pivoted line or plane, nested instances too, turns with it. Give a new plane or line a `guid` of your own to host forms on it in the same command; a plane or line a form or line is drawn on can't be deleted, and the datums can't be moved, changed or deleted. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A form's profile is its `sketch`, as Revit's Create Extrusion draws it: lines (`start` to `end`), arcs (`turn` degrees counter-clockwise from start to end; negative, clockwise) and whole circles (`centre`, `radius`), in any order, each number a number or a formula, joined end to end into loops: a loop inside another is a hole, several loops make one form of several solids; lines that don't close, cross or overlap are refused, named. A revolve's axis is a line of its sketch with `axis: true`, one at most. `profile` (corners in turn), `circle` and `axis` are shorthands, read as such lines. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load; both have a `system`. A `pipe` connector is where a pipe meets the family: its `domain` (cold or hot water, waste, vent, storm, gas), its `flow` (`in` as water into a basin, `out` as waste from a WC, `both` the default), `at` (where it is, mm, in the family's axes: x along it, y to its left, z up from its base), `direction` (the way the pipe leaves it, any length but none) and `size` (its DN, mm); a `data` or `earthing` connector has `at` and may have `direction` and `size`; an electrical one may have `at` and `direction`. Each of `at`, `direction` and `size` is a number or a formula over the family's parameters. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`, with `at` and `direction` in the model, where it stands; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out

commands.label: Add Family Parameters
commands.parameters: {families: [..], parameters: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material|text, instance?: true, value?, formula?, group?, definition?: GUID}]} new parameters added to each family, all or none. A type parameter's `value` is every type's until a type sets its own. `definition` ties it to a dictionary's or a project parameter's GUID, so a family's and the project's are one parameter. A name a family has already is skipped and listed

commands.label: Transfer Family Parameters
commands.parameters: {from, to: [families], names: [..], prefix?, suffix?, find?, replace?} a family's parameters copied to other families, with the parameters their formulas read, optionally renamed. A name a family has already is skipped and listed

commands.label: Favorites
commands.parameters: {action?: list|save|load|delete, kind?: material|family, name?, as?, replace?, path?} the user's favorites, kept in a file of their own (`path`; by default in their configuration folder) for every project to use: `save` the project's material or family `name` (a material with the picture its texture is made of, a family with the materials it is made of), under another name with `as`; `load` a favorite into the project, under another name with `as`, or over one it has already with `replace`; `delete` one from the favorites; `list` them (the default)

commands.label: Fill Patterns
commands.parameters: {name?, target?: drafting|model, lines?: [{angle, spacing, origin?: [x, y], shift?, dashes?: [mm, -mm, …]}, …], drawn?: scale | null, rename?, delete?: true} a fill pattern of the project's, as Revit's (and a PAT file's): families of parallel lines, each at `angle` degrees through `origin`, its lines `spacing` apart and each `shift` along from the last, whole or dashed (`dashes`: a dash's length, a space's as a negative one, 0 a dot); no lines, it fills solid. A drafting pattern's lengths are mm on paper, the same at any scale; a model pattern's mm in the building. A project starts with Solid fill, Diagonal Up and Down, Crosshatch, Diagonal Crosshatch, Horizontal, Vertical, Sand, Brick 225 x 75 and Tile 300. `rename` renames it, the region types filling with it following; `delete` takes it away while no type uses it. `drawn` is the scale (1 : n, its n) of the view one made of lines (`make_fill_pattern`) was drawn in: such a one given a new `target` and no `lines` is rescaled, a drafting one being the drawing on paper at that scale; null forgets it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern

commands.label: Filled Region
commands.parameters: {sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)

commands.label: Filled Region Types
commands.parameters: {name?, foreground?: pattern | null, foreground_color?, background?: pattern | null, background_color?, masking?, rename?, delete?: true} a filled region type of the project's: its foreground pattern over its background one, each in its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), over the paper when `masking` (it hides what's under it). A new one starts with none. A project starts with Solid Black, Diagonal Up, Crosshatch, Sand, Brick and Masking. `rename` renames it, its regions following; `delete` takes it away while no region is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

commands.label: Fillet Arc
commands.parameters: {ids: [a, b], radius} rounds the corner where two straight detail lines, or two straight walls, meet (or would, extended) with an arc of `radius` mm, in the first's line style or of the first's type: each is cut back to the arc

commands.label: View Filter
commands.parameters: {name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one

commands.label: Filter
commands.parameters: {ids: [id or GUID, …], by?, keep?: [value, …]} Revit's Filter on a selection: `groups` [{value, count, ids}, …], the values `by` takes among the elements (by default `Category`, whose values are categories' keys: wall, door, detail_line…; else a parameter as `fields` lists them, values as schedules show them, `""` for none), and `fields`, the parameters every one of them has, to filter by. With `keep`, `ids`: those holding one of its values, the selection to keep; it selects nothing itself, a front end does

commands.label: Flip
commands.parameters: {ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

commands.label: Floor
commands.parameters: {boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline

commands.label: Floor by Face
commands.parameters: {mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on

commands.label: Isolated Footing
commands.parameters: {at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below

commands.label: Project Location
commands.parameters: {crs?, eastings?, northings?, height?, rotation?, scale?, description?, geodetic_datum?, vertical_datum?, map_projection?, map_zone?, clear?: true} where the project lies on a map, as IFC's map conversion to a projected coordinate reference system: the CRS by name (an EPSG code, `EPSG:31983`; "" for none, a local grid) and what else is known of it, the map point of the project's internal origin (`eastings`, `northings`, `height`, mm), how far the project's x axis is turned from the map's east (`rotation`, degrees counterclockwise: true north east of project north) and a distance on the map over the same in the project (`scale`, 1 as it starts; in plan only, heights stay true). It is the active site: `location` names it and keeps others, and says it at the Survey Point. Any field makes one; what isn't given keeps its value. `clear` takes it away. With nothing, it says it (null for none). A projected EPSG code this version knows is the site's map system: it names itself as the description, and WGS84 (`convert_coordinates`, `location`'s `latitude` and `longitude`) and a map unit other than the metre go through it. `search` (with `limit`, 20 by default) finds systems whose code it is or whose name has all its words (`found`), and the countries and cities it names (`places`: "São Paulo", "paulo brasil", "Alemania", accents aside), each with its `longitude`, `latitude` and the `systems` surveys there use, the one to pick first: the national grid, the place's zone on the country's datum, the zone on WGS 84, each with `why`; it changes nothing. IFC import keeps the file's (moved with the model where the import brings it near the origin) and export writes it back as IfcMapConversion to an IfcProjectedCRS in metres; the model's own coordinates and drawings don't move

commands.label: Graphic Display Options
commands.parameters: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), edges?: true | false, silhouette?: px, ambient_shadows?: true | false} how a 3D view draws its edges and shadows, as Revit's Graphic Display Options: `edges`, the lines where its surfaces meet in Shaded (on unless turned off; Hidden Line always draws them); `silhouette`, an outline that many pixels wide (a whole number, 0 to 10; 0, the default, for none) round what stands in front of what is further off or of nothing; `ambient_shadows`, soft shadows where faces meet inside a corner (off unless turned on). What is left out stays as it was; with none of them it only says what the view has

commands.label: Visibility/Graphics
