commands.parameters: {view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, orientation?: project_north|true_north (a plan's: which north is up; true north turns it on screen by the active location's angle to true north, never the model), reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines); under doors and windows, `dooropening` and `windowopening` (a door's swing, a window's opening lines: the family symbols that name the subcategory `Opening`). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)

commands.label: Grid
commands.parameters: {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

commands.label: Earthing Conductor
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)

commands.label: Detail Groups
commands.parameters: {name?, rename?, delete?: true} a detail group type: `rename` renames it, its groups following; `delete` takes it away while none of it is placed. Without `name`, it lists each with its members and how many are placed

commands.label: Synthetic Highrise
commands.parameters: {storeys?: 20} replace the project with an original 1–80 storey performance sample

commands.label: Size Hydrants
commands.parameters: {column?: 1-5, area?, type?: 1|2|3|4-40|4-65|5, hydrants?, inside?, nominal?, material?: steel|steel-wet|copper|pvc|pex, length?, rise?} hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks. With `column` (of Tabela 3, by the occupation) and `area` (m², built) it replies the system type and the fire reserve (m³). With `type` (Tabela 2; 4 comes as 4-40 or 4-65 by its nozzle) it replies the design flow, that of the two most unfavourable jets (`hydrants`, 2 by default), and the head at the nozzle; with `inside` (mm) it also replies the speed (5 m/s at most), the Hazen-Williams head loss over `length` (m) of the `material` (Tabela 1: `steel` is black steel in a dry system, C 100, the lowest steel row and the default, `steel-wet` is galvanised or wet, C 120), the head needed at the start of the pipe with its `rise` (mm, up) and, with `nominal` (mm), whether the pipe is big enough (DN 65; DN 50 for types 1 and 2). `length` and `rise` are in millimetres. `need_mca` is the nozzle head + the head loss of the straight pipe + the rise: it leaves out the hose, the fittings and the pressure at the source (`need_covers` says so), and `ok` is only the nozzle head within 100 mca, the speed and the pipe's size (`ok_covers`), not a verdict on the design. A `type` that contradicts `column` and `area` is an error. Notes 1 and 2 of Tabela 3 (a system one type lower in some cases) are not applied. `region` is SP, the only one: this is the São Paulo rule, and no other state's. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: IDs of Selection
commands.parameters: {ids: [id or GUID, …]} what names each element: its `id`, its `guid`, its `ifc` GlobalId, its `category` and its `name` (or type, number, mark)

commands.label: Import CAD
commands.parameters: {path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, acquire?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given), origin (its origin on `at`) or shared (where its coordinates, the map's, put it by the active location, turned and scaled to match; `acquire: true` first sets the location from the drawing, so its middle lands at the origin); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out

commands.label: Import Fill Patterns
commands.parameters: {path | text, replace?: false} the fill patterns of a PAT file (AutoCAD's and Revit's), from the file at `path` or as `text`: each `*Name` and its families of lines, in mm unless the file says `;%UNITS=INCH`, drafting unless a pattern says `;%TYPE=MODEL`. A pattern the project already has is left as it is unless `replace`; one that can't be a pattern (no lines, an offset of 0, dashes that are all spaces, too many families) is left out. A file is read up to its first 2000 patterns. It returns those `imported`, those `left_out` (the first 100, each with why) and `left_out_count`, all of them

commands.label: Import Mesh
commands.parameters: {path, level?, at?: [x, y], units?, up?} brings in the 3D objects of an OBJ (with the MTL library it names) or a glTF 2.0 (`.gltf` with its buffers, or `.glb`): each object of the file (an OBJ's `o` or `g`, a glTF's node with a mesh) a Generic Model family of its name, made of its triangles grouped by material, and placed where the file has it, on `level` (the lowest by default) with the file's origin on `at` (the project's origin unless given). `units` of an OBJ: mm, cm, m (the default), in or ft; `up`, the axis its file stands on: y (the default, as most programs write OBJ) or z. A glTF is in metres with y up, as its specification says. The file's materials come in with their colours and opacity, where the project has none of their name. Returns `components` and `families` made and what was `left_out` (lines and points, textures, a compressed mesh, an object past what a family may hold)

commands.label: Insert from File
commands.parameters: {path, ids?: [id, …], same_parameters?: [name, …]} elements of another project (.bimc, .bimcraft or .ifc) brought into this one: those `ids` names (their ids there), else all of them, and what they point at that this project hasn't (a level they stand on is this project's of the same name, where it has one). Each keeps its id unless this project has that id, and its GUID unless this project has that GUID: then it's a copy, with a GUID of its own (the same file inserted into itself is copied whole). What they point at among themselves follows them. A name or a number taken here gets ` 2`, ` 3`…; types, families, materials and parameters this project hasn't come by name, and so do the line styles (with their line patterns), fill patterns, filled region types and detail groups a detail line, a filled region or a group uses. Returns `ids` {there: here}, `copies`, `library`, `left_out`

commands.label: Inspect
commands.parameters: {brief?} levels, element counts, types, warnings and undo history; with `brief` the library is its size only (`library`), not its types, materials, families, parameters and images, which is most of the answer

commands.label: Join into Polyline
commands.parameters: {ids: [id, …]} joins detail lines of one view, lines, arcs and polylines that meet end to end, into one polyline in the first's line style (closed when they come round); the first keeps its id, the rest are deleted, and a dimension that measured one of the rest loses that reference (and is deleted, left with fewer than two): the reply's `notes` say which

commands.label: Project Language
commands.parameters: {code?: en|pt|es|sv|cs|fr|de|nl|it|pl|vi} the language the project's drawings speak (a stair's UP, a title block's SCALE, a schedule's headings) and new names come in (levels, sections, elevations, sheets, rooms, schedules): English, Brazilian Portuguese, Spanish, Swedish, Czech, French, German, Dutch, Italian, Polish or Vietnamese. What's already named stays named

commands.label: Level
commands.parameters: {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]], elevation_base?: base|survey} a level at an elevation in mm (internal); `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it); `elevation_base`, what its head shows its elevation from: the Project Base Point (the default) or the Survey Point, the shared coordinates

commands.label: Library
commands.parameters: {kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too

commands.label: Line Patterns
commands.parameters: {name?, segments?: [{dash: mm} | {space: mm} | "dot" | {dot_length: mm} | {offset: {length, count, distance}} | {wave: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {zigzag: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {text: {length, size, text}}, …], rename?, delete?: true} a line pattern of the project's: 1–32 freely ordered graphic segments, each 0.05–100 mm long on paper, so it reads the same at any scale. Offsets have 2–9 lines spaced symmetrically; frequency is cycles per segment, 0.1–100; amplitude and spacing are mm. Text uses bundled IBM Plex Sans, size is maximum capital height (shrinks to fit length), 1–256 single-line characters, following the curve. All graphics preserve the centerline. A project starts with Dash, Long Dash, Dot, Dash Dot, Hidden and Centre; Solid is a line with none. `rename` renames it, the line styles using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no style uses it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern

commands.label: Line Styles
commands.parameters: {name?, pen?, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], pattern?: name | "Solid", rename?, delete?: true} a line style of the project's, as Revit's: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) its lines draw in, their colour (black unless told) and their line pattern. A new one needs `pen`; one changed keeps what it isn't given. A project starts with Hairline, Thin Lines, Medium Lines, Wide Lines, Hidden Lines, Centre Lines and Overhead Lines. `rename` renames it, the lines drawn in it following; `delete` takes it away, while no line is drawn in it. Without `name`, it lists every style

commands.label: Line Weights
commands.parameters: {model?: [{scale, widths}, …], annotation?: [16 widths], reset?: true} the project's line weights, as Revit's Manage > Line Weights: what each pen draws on paper, mm. `model` gives, whole, the model's pens 1 to 16 at each of its scales (1 to 32 of them, 1 : `scale`): a view draws its walls, doors, patterns and the rest of the model in the column of the scale nearest its own (by how many times finer or coarser; the finer of two as near). `annotation` gives the 16 pens that dimensions, tags, text, grids, levels and marks draw in, at any scale. Each width is 0.01 to 20 mm; pen 0 is always a hairline. `reset` goes back to what a project in its units starts with (the model's pens wider at finer scales; at 1 : 100, pen 4 is 0.18 mm and pen 10 0.35 mm). Without any, it says what they are, each scale named as the project's units name it, and `own` whether the project has set them

commands.label: Linework
commands.parameters: {view?, id, at: [x, y], style? | invisible?: true, remove?: true} Revit's Linework: the edge of element `id` that a plan (`view`, a level's or a plan view; the lowest level's by default) draws nearest `at` (within 200 mm), drawn in that view only in line style `style`, or not at all with `invisible`; `remove` takes the Linework nearest `at` off that edge again (one edge, even where another lies within reach; where that edge has none, the nearest entry within reach on an edge the element no longer draws, one a call). A view holds at most 2000 edges. It returns the edge, `from` and `to`, or with `remove` how many were `removed`

commands.label: Link Model
commands.parameters: {path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees, by?: manual|base|shared, location?} another project (.bimc, .bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. `by: base` puts its Project Base Point on this project's (turned `angle` about it, and raised to it); `by: shared` stands it where its shared coordinates say (its active location, or `location`), by this project's active location: worked out each time it is drawn, never written into its file. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`, and where it stands: `at`, `angle`, `raised`

commands.label: Residential Load Points
commands.parameters: {rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?, standard?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The numbers are data (`data/load-points.json`, one rule set for each standard, every row naming its source): `standard` names the set, `NBR 5410:2004` the default and only one so far, and the answer gives `standard`, `standard_source`, `lighting_source` and each room's `source`. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish, with the power outlets and the luminaires that stand in each (the room a component's point is in, at the walls' centre lines; standing in the last phase, primary design options): `tug_points` and `lighting_points` are those drawn, and a room with no luminaire is not `ok`. Where the model draws no outlet, or no luminaire, at all, that count is the least instead (`counted` says which were drawn). A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Location
commands.parameters: {name?, east?, north?, elevation?, latitude?, longitude?, angle?, scale?, crs?, rename?, activate?: true, delete?: true, shift?: [de, dn, dz]} a named site of the project (Revit's), one position of the building in the shared coordinates: the Survey Point's shared `east`, `north` and `elevation` (mm), or its `latitude` and `longitude` through the site's map system, the `angle` from project north to true north (degrees, east positive) and the `scale` from ground to grid (1 unless a map projection's; heights are not scaled), and its map system (`crs`, as `georeference` takes it). The active site is the georeference; the others are kept beside it, each where it would put the project. A new one starts as a copy of the active one. `activate` makes it the active one, the georeference. `shift` adds to its east, north and elevation, or to every site's when no `name` is given (the survey says the site is 5 m higher: shift [0, 0, 5000]). The active site can't be deleted. Without `name` or `shift`, lists them

commands.label: Make Fill Pattern
commands.parameters: {ids, from: [x, y], to: [x, y], name, target?: model|drafting} a fill pattern made of the detail lines `ids` (all of one view), as pyRevit's Make Pattern makes one: the rectangle between corners `from` and `to` (in the view's terms) is the tile the pattern repeats, and what of the lines lies outside it is cut off. Each line becomes a family that runs on into the next tiles' copies of itself; one at a slope that never meets itself again is turned to the simplest slope within 0.25° that does (else the nearest, at most 48 tiles across or up). A model pattern (the default) is as drawn; a drafting one is the drawing on paper, at the view's scale. The tile is 0.05 to 100000 each way, and holds at most 256 lines. It returns the pattern's `name` and the `pattern`

commands.label: Mass
commands.parameters: {boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`

commands.label: Mass Floors
commands.parameters: {mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level

commands.label: Match Properties
commands.parameters: {from: id, ids: [id,…]} gives the elements in `ids` the type of `from` (and, for components, its family), as Revit's Match Properties does; only elements of `from`'s category take it, the rest come back in `skipped`. Returns {modified, skipped}

commands.label: Materials
commands.parameters: {name, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], transparency?: 0-100, cut?, surface?, texture?: {kind?, size?: [w, h], angle?, offset?: [x, y], path?, image?} | null, rename?, delete?: true} a material of the project's library, created or changed: its colour in shaded 3D views, its `transparency` there (percent of what lies behind it that shows through, 0 opaque; the starter Glass has 70), the pattern its cut shows in plans and sections (where a layer is wide enough to hold it), and the one its surfaces show at its size in the building (a floor's top in plan, a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan). Patterns: none, solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete, insulation, or the name of one of the project's fill patterns (see `fill_pattern`), kept while the material shows it and renamed with it. Its `texture` is what its surfaces look like in the 3D view, over its colour, a tile of it `size` mm across and up, turned `angle` degrees and moved `offset` mm: a pattern drawn in code, `kind` brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof, fabric, metal or insulation (at its natural size unless `size` says); or `image`, a picture: the PNG or JPEG file at `path`, taken into the project (up to 1024 px a side, 24 pictures), or one the project holds (`image`, its id from `inspect`); null takes the texture away. `rename` renames it, the layers using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no layer uses it. `inspect` lists the library and the pictures

commands.label: Mirror
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

commands.label: Modify
commands.parameters: {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. `join: false` on a wall or a run turns off its joins: its ends stay square and it neither stretches with its neighbours nor pulls them (Revit's Disallow Join). A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

commands.label: Move
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall or one run moves. One section or elevation takes `end` as the part its grips in plan move: `line` (the line it starts at, the way it looks), `start` or `end` (an end along the line, while it is cropped), `far` (its far clip, changing `depth`) and, an elevation, `mark` (its mark alone, anywhere: past its reference it turns round and its line comes over)

commands.label: Pipe Network
commands.parameters: {system?, level?, tolerance?} the pipe network, worked out from the model and never stored: where pipes' ends and the pipe connectors of fixtures, fittings and valves meet. Points within `tolerance` mm (1 by default, 50 at most) are one node; a pipe's end or a connector on another pipe's length is a node too, splitting that pipe into two edges (the element stays whole); a fitting's or a valve's connectors are joined through it, a fixture's are not (its waste and its water are networks of their own). `system` keeps the networks that pipe system's pipes are in; `level` (a name, id or GUID) only that level's pipes and components. It replies `nodes` (`at`, what meets there: a pipe's `start` or `end`, a pipe `along` which it lies, a component's `connector` and its `domain`), `edges` (a pipe's piece and its `length`, or `through` a fitting), `groups` (the elements joined together, their pipes' systems and their connectors' domains), `open` (ends and connectors that meet nothing, as Revit's Show Disconnects marks) and `warnings`, which never refuse the model: `systems_meet` (pipes of two systems in one network), `domains_meet` (connectors of two domains, waste and cold water), `joined_mid_run` (a pipe met along its length, with no fitting) and `smaller_downstream` (in a network with a waste connector, a pipe leaving a node downhill narrower than one coming down to it). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: New
commands.parameters: {name?, language?: en|pt|es|sv|cs|fr|de|nl|it|pl|vi} an empty project with Level 1 (0) and Level 2 (3000), named in its language (Nível 1, Nível 2 in Portuguese; Nivel 1, Nivel 2 in Spanish; Nivå 1, Nivå 2 in Swedish; Niveau 1, Niveau 2 in Dutch; Tầng 1, Tầng 2 in Vietnamese)

commands.label: Object Styles
commands.parameters: {categories?: {category: {projection?: pen, cut?: pen}, …}, reset?: true} the project's object styles, as Revit's Manage > Object Styles: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) each model category draws its lines in where it is seen (`projection`) and where a view cuts it (`cut`), in every plan and section; a view's Visibility/Graphics overrides them. A category given keeps the pen it isn't given. The rest of an element's lines keep their own: a compound wall's layers, a door's jambs, a stair's walk line. `reset` goes back to what a project starts with (cut pen 10 and seen pen 4; a door's and a window's cut 6, a railing seen 6, a mass 4 both). Without either, it says each model category's, `own` whether the project has set it apart. A door's and a window's subcategory `dooropening` and `windowopening` (the swing, the opening lines) are rows too, drawing in their category's pens until given their own

commands.label: Offset
commands.parameters: {id, distance, toward: [x, y], copy?} a detail line drawn again `distance` mm beside itself on the side `toward` is, arcs round the same centres, an ellipse or a spline as a spline through points within 0.05 mm of the true offset (which Revit can't): a copy (the default), or with `copy` false moved

commands.label: Design Options
commands.parameters: {set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)

commands.label: Paint
commands.parameters: {id | ids, face?, material} paints a face of the elements with a material of the library, as Revit's Paint does: its colour and texture show in the 3D view over what their types are made of. `face`: a wall's `exterior` or `interior`, a floor's, roof's or ceiling's `top` or `bottom`, and `all` for a column, a component, a door, a window, a stair, a ramp or a railing; without it, every face the elements have. `material` null takes the paint off

commands.label: Panel
commands.parameters: {id?, distribution?, mains?, slots?, supply_from?} the electrical data of a distribution board, an equipment component: `distribution` one of the project's distribution systems (`distribution_system` lists them), `mains` the main breaker in amperes, `slots` how many single-pole breakers it takes (Max #1 Pole Breakers) and `supply_from` the board that supplies it, by id or GUID: boards make a tree, and a supply loop is refused. What isn't given stays; "" takes one away. Without `id`, lists the boards with what each feeds. A board's `12 circuits`, `24 circuits` and `36 circuits` are its size, not its slots

commands.label: Panel Schedule
commands.parameters: {panel: id, name?, template?: branch|list, show_spare?, show_space?, phase_columns?, scale?, notes?} makes the panel schedule (quadro de cargas) of a distribution board: a view that goes on a sheet with `place` and prints with it, listed in the Project Browser and by `inspect`. It has the board's header (system, voltage, phases, mains, level), a row for each of its slots (`Max #1 Pole Breakers`; a circuit takes the slots `number`, `number`+2… for as many poles, each on a phase, A B C repeating every two slots), a spare (a breaker with no device) and a space (a slot no circuit takes) drawn differently, the load by classification (the project's `demand_factors` applied) and by phase (the phases add up to the board's load, the current of a phase its demand over the phase voltage), and `notes`. `template` is the branch panel's two columns or a list; `show_spare` and `show_space` (true) show the rows; `phase_columns` (true) a column for each phase; `scale` (1) how large it comes out.

commands.label: Project Parameters
commands.parameters: {name, kind?: text|number|integer|length|area|volume|angle|yesno, categories?: [wall|floor|ceiling|roof|door|window|room|column|component|stair|ramp|railing|mass, …], sets?: {category: property set name|null}, classification?: {system, edition?}|null, rename?, delete?: true, description?, group?, read_only?: bool, scope?: instance|type, dictionary?: null} a project parameter, as Revit's Manage > Project Parameters makes one: a value of its kind each element of its categories may have of its own, set with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}`, or, `scope` type, each of their types, set with `type_parameter`. Rooms, stairs, ramps and masses have no types. Made a type parameter, its elements' values are wiped (answers `wiped`); made an instance parameter, each type's value is copied to its elements (`copied`). (Lengths in mm, areas in m², volumes in m³, angles in degrees, yes or no as true or false.) Off a category, that category's elements lose their values of it; deleted, every element does; renamed, they follow it, as schedules, their formulas, filters and tags do. `sets` names the IFC property set a category's values go in (an import keeps the one they came in; none: `Project Parameters`); `classification` makes a text parameter a classification system's codes, which IFC holds as classification references. `group` (one of Revit's, or a name of the project's own) and `read_only` are how Properties shows it. `dictionary` null makes one from a dictionary a project parameter again. `parameter_list` lists them

commands.label: Parameter Batch
commands.parameters: {ops: [{op?: set, …`parameter`'s params} | {op: delete, name} | {op: duplicate, name, as?} | {op: rename, names: [..], prefix?, suffix?, find?, replace?}], dry_run?: true} several changes to project parameters, all or none and one undo step. A duplicate is a parameter of its own, with its own GUID; its values don't come with it. `dry_run` says what would be done and changes nothing

commands.label: Export Parameters
commands.parameters: {path, names?: [..], definitions?: [..], name?, version?} the project's parameters, those named, or the `definitions` given, to a .xlsx or .csv table or a .bimparams dictionary (with its `name` and `version`). Definitions only, not values. Revit's shared parameter .txt is read, not written

commands.label: Import Parameters
commands.parameters: {path, dry_run?: true, map?: {their category: ours | null}, categories?: [..], resolve?: {name: same|separate|skip}, scopes?: {name: instance|type}, names?: [..], replace_categories?: true, skip_conflicts?: true} parameter definitions from a .xlsx or .csv table (columns GUID, Name, Kind, Categories, Group, Description, Instance/Type, User Modifiable), a .bimparams dictionary or a Revit shared parameter .txt. Answers each row's status: `create`, `modify`, `existing`, `conflict` or `skip`, with notes; `dry_run` stops there. A row is matched by GUID first, so it follows a rename; one of a name taken by another GUID is a conflict until `resolve` says `same` (the file's GUID means that parameter from now on), `separate` (it comes in as `name 2`) or `skip`. The file's categories are matched by name, Revit's among them, and `map` settles the ones listed as `unmapped` and is kept with the project; `broad` lists those that land on a wider category (all components). `categories` is for rows that name none, as a shared parameter file's. A file adds categories unless `replace_categories`. A conflict stops the import unless `skip_conflicts`. No element's values come from the file

commands.label: Parameter List
commands.parameters: {} every project parameter with its id, GUID, whether it is shared (from a dictionary), its settings and what uses it (values, schedules, view filters, tags, calculated fields); the dictionaries in use and the category mapping kept

commands.label: Merge Parameters
commands.parameters: {from, into, overwrite?: true} parameter `from`'s values, and the schedules, filters, tags and formulas that name it, moved to `into`, of the same kind; `from` goes, and files holding its GUID mean `into` from then on. Elements holding both with different values stop it unless `overwrite` takes `from`'s

commands.label: Purge Parameters
commands.parameters: {dry_run?: true} takes out the project parameters nothing uses (no value, schedule, view filter, tag or calculated field); answers the names

commands.label: Perspective
commands.parameters: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands

commands.label: Phasing
commands.parameters: {name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides

commands.label: Phase Filter
commands.parameters: {name, new?, existing?, demolished?, temporary?, delete?} a phase filter: how a view shows each status of what's in its phase, each `by-category` (as its category and the view's overrides say), `overridden` (as the project's overrides for that status say) or `not-displayed`. A project has Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New; any may change. A new one starts by category throughout. One in use by a view or a template can't be deleted. Replies with the filter

commands.label: Pin
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…]} pins elements where they are: `move`, `rotate`, `mirror`, `align`, `delete`, `flip`, `split`, `corner`, `trim_extend`, `fillet`, `offset` with `copy` false and the detail line tools refuse them until `unpin`. A pinned element is marked `pinned` in `elements` and kept in the file. Returns {pinned: [ids]}

commands.label: Pipe
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")

commands.label: Place View
commands.parameters: {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`; an unscaled 3D view uses the finest offered project scale from the default up that fits the sheet's room, or the coarsest if none fits; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default in a free spot clear of the other views, their titles and the title block, or in the title block's drawing area; right of all views when full); a view goes on one sheet. Returns {id, at, scale}, and a `warning` when the view or its title reaches past the paper. Told a scale of its own, the viewport keeps it whatever the view's later changes, until `modify {follow_scale: true}`, which gives it the view's scale again, whatever `scale` comes with it. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

commands.label: Point Cloud
commands.parameters: {path | cloud, name?, level?, at?: [x, y], offset?, angle?, units?, spacing?, origin?, acquire?} brings in a laser scan (`path`: PTS, XYZ, PLY, LAS or E57 (each of its scans placed by its pose), or a list of the files of one scan's stations, brought in as one; `units` of its coordinates mm, cm, m (the default), in or ft; one point kept in each cube `spacing` mm wide) or places one the project holds again (`cloud`, its name), as an element: its middle on `at` (the origin) and its foot on the level, or with `origin: file` where its file's coordinates put it, or with `origin: shared` where they put it as the map's, by the active location (`acquire: true` first sets the location from the scan, so its middle lands at the origin and its foot on 0); `offset` raises its middle over the level, `angle` turns it. Returns its id, the scan's name, the points kept and read, and where its middle was in the file

commands.label: View/Sheet Set
commands.parameters: {name?, views?: [id, GUID, view name or sheet number, …], add?: [...], remove?: [...], rename?, delete?: true} a print set, as Revit's View/Sheet Set: a named list of views and sheets (plans, sections, elevations, 3D views, schedules and sheets, any mix) printed or exported together, in the order given. `views` gives the whole list (a new set needs it, empty or not), `add` and `remove` change it. A view deleted leaves every set. Without `name`, lists the sets, each its views' ids and titles

commands.label: Project Information
commands.parameters: {name?, number?, client?, address?, status?, issue_date?, author?, organization?, organization_description?, building?, params?: {parameter: value | null}}: the project's information, as Revit's Project Information. Each field is text (`""` empties it; only `address` has lines, by `\n`); `name` is the project's name. `params` sets its values of the project parameters for category `project` (null takes one away), as `modify` does on its element. With nothing, answers what it holds: {id (none until something is set), name, the fields, params}. Sheets' title blocks show the number, client, status and issue date; IFC writes the status as the project's phase, the building's name and address, and the rest in property sets

commands.label: Property Line
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], name?, level?} a named closed property boundary (mm), on the lowest level unless given. A repeated closing point is accepted. The outline must be simple, without crossings, spikes or repeated corners. Plans draw a dash-dot boundary with its name and area. `elements` gives area_m2, perimeter_m and segments (length in mm, bearing in survey quadrants, azimuth clockwise from north: the map's, turned by the georeference's `rotation`; without one, the project's +y). Schedules list name, area and perimeter. IFC writes closed curves in the site's FootPrint. Returns id, name, area_m2

commands.label: Publish
commands.parameters: {name, folder?} writes publishing set `name` (`publish_set`) out: each of its folders' print sets as its format, under the set's own folder (beside the project's file unless absolute) or under `folder` when given. Returns what `export` returns: `written` (each file's path, format and what it is of), `failed` (what wasn't written and why; the rest go on) and `cancelled`

commands.label: Publisher
commands.parameters: {name?, folder?, folders?: [{name, entries: [{print_set, format, name?, combine?, options?}]}], overwrite?: true, timings?, rename?, duplicate?, delete?: true} a publishing set, the Publisher's preset: folders that hold print sets (`print_set`), each written as a `format` (an id or an extension from `export_formats`). A print set may be in a folder once for each format. `folder` is where the set is written: beside the project's file unless absolute. A folder's `name` is under it (a `/` nests, none is the destination itself). An entry's `name` is its files' template (the tokens `export` takes, and `{PrintSet}`, `{PublishSet}`, Project Information's fields as `{Project Number}`, `{Client Name}`…, and any project parameter by its name); `combine` names the one file all of the set's views go in (PDF); `options`: {page?, pdf?, quality?, ifc_origin?} as `export` takes them. `folders` gives them all (a new set may have none); `duplicate` makes a copy of `name` called that. A print set deleted leaves every folder. Without `name`, lists the sets. `timings` records completed entry exports, each with folder, print_set, format and time {started_ms, ended_ms, duration_ms}. `publish` writes one

commands.label: Purge Unused
commands.parameters: {kinds?: [type|family|material|picture|filter|template|titleblock, …], dry_run?} takes out what nothing uses, again for what that leaves unused: types and families unless `kinds` says; a category keeps a type and a family a type; with `dry_run` it lists what would go and changes nothing

commands.label: Railing
commands.parameters: {host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are

commands.label: Ramp
commands.parameters: {start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level

commands.label: Rebar
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule

commands.label: Recover Autosave
commands.parameters: {path, project?} open and validate a recovery snapshot; Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it

commands.label: Redo
commands.parameters: {count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default). In a Co-Work session, the caller's own last `count` undos

commands.label: Reference Plane
commands.parameters: {start, end, up?: [x,y,z], name?, level?} a reference plane of the project: drawn along the line from `start` to `end` ([x, y] on `level`, the lowest by default, or [x, y, z]), its other direction `up` (the vertical by default, so a line drawn in plan makes an upright plane; tilt `up` for a sloped one). Work plane-based components are placed on it (`component` `host`) and move with it; deleting it deletes them. A name is one plane's

commands.label: Reinforce
commands.parameters: {host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes

commands.label: Reinforcement Presets
commands.parameters: {name?, kind?: beam|column|footing|floor, params?, rename?, delete?: true} a named set of the parameters `reinforce` takes for one kind of host (`params`: its `cover`, `grade`, `grade_stirrup`, `clearance` and what its kind takes, and not `host`), kept in the project; `reinforce` with `preset` takes it and lets what is given with it replace its own. Without `name`, lists them. It is not checked against any host until it arms one

commands.label: Reload Links
commands.parameters: {id?} read the file of the link `id`, or of every link, again: for a project that changed on disk. Returns `reloaded` (the names) and `failed` ({name, error})

commands.label: Reload CAD
commands.parameters: {cad} reads a linked CAD drawing's file again, so every import of it shows what the file holds now (opening the project does too). Returns whether it changed

commands.label: Rename Type
commands.parameters: {category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type, name} renames a type of a category (`category` and `type`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`) to `name`, as Rename in Type Properties does: the elements of it, and what else names it, follow, and it keeps its GUID; refused for a name another type of it has. Text types and filled region types rename with `rename` on `text_type` and `filled_region_type`

commands.label: Render
commands.parameters: {family?, type?, mode?: 3d|plan|elevation, wall_thickness?, view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, a sheet's number, or {3D}, ceiling?, width?, height?, path?, azimuth?, elevation?, eye_elevation?} a family on its own with `family` — its `type` (the first by default) standing in a model of its own, in a wall `wall_thickness` mm thick (200) if it's a door's or a window's, nothing of this project's touched or left behind: `3d` (as seen from the south-east), `plan` (what its symbols draw) or `elevation` (front-on, as seen from the north), a PNG as `pngBase64` or at `path`. Without it: a level's floor plan (with `ceiling`, its reflected ceiling plan, looking up from 2300 mm), a section, an elevation, a sheet (at 5 px a paper mm), or the 3D view seen from `azimuth` degrees round from east (counter-clockwise) and `elevation` degrees up (by default from the south-east, 30° up), fitted; in perspective (see `perspective`) through its lens, and with `eye_elevation` from an eye that high (mm) looking at the same point, as a PNG (pngBase64), or written to a path: .png, .svg for a plan, .pdf for a sheet. A plan, section, elevation or sheet that could not draw something as asked (a fill pattern too dense for the view, more ink behind a region than is kept above it, or unsupported drawing lettering replaced with a question mark) says so in the reply's `notes`

commands.label: Repeating Detail
commands.parameters: {type, start: [x,y], end: [x,y], spacing, mirrored?, view?} detail group `type` repeated along the line from `start` to `end`, every `spacing` mm from `start` (at most 2000 of them), each turned along the line, as Revit's Repeating Detail Component: brick coursing, blocking, batt ties. A view draws up to 10000 group members in all (a repeat places each member of the type again), so a type of 100 members repeats up to 100 times. Returns {id, count}

commands.label: Size Water Reservation
commands.parameters: {daily_l? | people?, per_person_l?, days?, fire_l?, house?, lower_percent?, compartments?, fill_flow?, pumps?, towers?, smallest_l?, peak_l?} the reservation of a building as NBR 5626:2020 asks. The day's consumption is `daily_l` (litres), or `people` times `per_person_l`: the standard gives no litres per person, so it is the project's own assumption and the reply says so. The potable volume is `days` of it (1 by default, 24 h being the least; 3 at most unless the project shows how the quality is kept) and `fire_l` is kept apart and added (the project's and the fire brigade's, not the standard's). The reply has the refill flow (the day's consumption in 6 h, or 3 h with `house`, a single-family house) and checks each of one kind (current requirement, historical reference, engineering practice, configurable assumption): `fill_flow` (L/s) against that flow, `compartments` of an elevated reservoir (2 at least, a house excepted), `smallest_l` against `peak_l` (the greatest peak over a normal maintenance), `pumps` (2 independent at least) and, with `towers` of 2 or more, the spare pump. A check whose input is not given is `pending` and never stops the others; `ok` is that none failed. `lower_percent` splits the potable volume between the lower and the upper reservoir, a choice of the project's; the usual split is only a suggestion. It leaves out the pump's head and the recalque pipe. It changes nothing

commands.label: Reset Shape
commands.parameters: {id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again

commands.label: Roof
commands.parameters: {level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces; over an explicit `boundary` or `sketch`, eaves `overhang` mm (0) beyond the drawn wall line, the base at it. Round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it): flat at `slope` 0, else every edge sloping up at `slope` degrees (30), hips, valleys and ridges where the slopes meet, but the edges in `gables` (edge i runs from point i to the next, the courtyards' edges numbered on after the boundary's) left upright, gable ends; `gable` leaves a rectangle's short ends upright. `slopes`: a slope in degrees (up to 75) for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for an edge that takes `slope`; none, every edge does; the eaves stay level and an edge in `gables` stays upright whatever its slope. A `sketch` line may carry a `slope` for the edges along it. Or with `extrusion` {line: [[x,y],[x,y]], profile: [[along, up],…], from?, to}: its underside's profile in the upright plane through `line`, along it from its start and up from the base, swept square to it from `from` (0) to `to` mm to its left. `openings` are holes through it in plan; with `join`, a roof it runs into, it ends where it meets that one's top

commands.label: Roof by Face
commands.parameters: {mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on

commands.label: Room
commands.parameters: {point: [x,y], level?, type?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

commands.label: Area and Volume Computations
commands.parameters: {at?: centre|finish} where the project measures its rooms' areas, perimeters and IFC spaces, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations: at the walls' centre lines (`centre`, as a project starts) or at their finish faces (`finish`, the floor inside the walls: the área útil Brazilian codes ask for). Rooms keep their points; only their measured outline changes. IFC spaces carry both areas in Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities whichever is chosen

commands.label: Room Finish
commands.parameters: {id, part?: floor|ceiling, action: disconnect|regenerate} a room's own floor or ceiling, the one its type makes for it (`type {category: room, floor, ceiling}`) and keeps along its boundary at the walls' faces. `id` is the room (then `part` says which) or the floor or the ceiling itself. `disconnect` lets it go: it stays as it is, an ordinary floor or ceiling that can be edited freely, and nothing connects it again. `regenerate` makes a new one for a room whose own was disconnected or deleted. While connected, its outline, level, type and offset are the room's: `edit_boundary` and `modify` of those are refused, and moved, it is put back. `elements` gives a room's `floor` and `ceiling` ({connected: guid}, or disconnected) and a connected floor's or ceiling's `room`

commands.label: Room Separator
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

commands.label: Rotate
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

commands.label: Rotate Project North
commands.parameters: {angle?: degrees, true_north?: true, about?: [x, y]} turns the whole model `angle` degrees counter-clockwise about `about` (default the Project Base Point), as Revit's Rotate Project North: every element that has a place in plan, the Project Base Point and the Survey Point, and links placed by hand or by base points; and turns every location's angle back by as much, so nothing moves in the world, only the project's axes. `true_north: true` turns it by the active location's angle, so project north is true north. Returns the `angle` turned and the elements `rotated`

commands.label: Save
commands.parameters: {path?, ifc_origin?, compress?} .bimc saves the project (Save As with a path), as does .bimt (a template): compact JSON, or with `compress: true` the same JSON in a zip of one entry, `project.json`, deflated on every core (several times smaller, slower to save and open; a .json path is always plain; `open` reads either); .ifc exports IFC4, its coordinates' origin at `ifc_origin`: internal (the default), base (the Project Base Point), survey (the Survey Point) or shared (the map's coordinates themselves), with the active location's IfcMapConversion and IfcProjectedCRS, true north, and the site's latitude and longitude where the project has a CRS; .glb exports the default 3D view's scene as glTF 2.0 (metres, y up, a node for each element named by its id, GUID and category in `extras`; returns `elements` and `triangles`); .svg or .png exports the lowest level's plan; .pdf prints every sheet, a page each

commands.label: View Scale
commands.parameters: {view, scale?: 1 | … | 100000} a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, 1 : `scale`: the paper the view stands for, 1 mm of paper being `scale` mm of the model. Its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, tags, dimension ticks…) and its line weights (pens) are that paper's, so a screen shows them as the paper would at its zoom. Every view has one: 1 : 100 until it is given another, and null is refused. A view placed on a sheet takes it for the viewport's scale, and the viewports of it there follow when it changes, unless one was placed at a scale of its own. Without `scale` it only says what the view has

commands.label: Schedule
commands.parameters: {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings, levels or sheets, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; none, every built one but rooms, levels, masses and sheets), with the fields they share (Category, Family, Type, Level, Count, Width, Height, Length, Thickness, Area: a wall's length by its height, a door's width by its height; Material: its type's structure layer's, a run's type's, a family's), each empty where its category has none; `category` alone reads its own (Room Schedule, Door Schedule, Window Schedule, Wall Schedule, Floor Schedule, Level Schedule, Sheet List, each the project's once changed). `fields`: its columns, in order, each a field's name (`available` lists them: its category's own, Count, project parameters, a component's family's parameters) or {name, formula?, kind?: number|length|area|yesno, heading?, total?}; with a formula, a calculated field worked out from the row's other fields as a family's formulas are (lengths in mm, areas in m²; `Area * 120`); `total` sums it in a totals row. `filters`: [{field, op: equals|not-equals|greater|greater-or-equal|less|less-or-equal|contains|not-contains|begins-with|not-begins-with|ends-with|not-ends-with|has-value|has-no-value, value}, …], the elements all of them keep (text in any case, numbers as the schedule shows them, an unset yes or no as no). `sort`: [field or {field, descending?}, …], in turn (its first column unless it says; Phase Created and Phase Demolished in the project's order of phases, a phase never demolished after the last); `grouped`, a row for each set of the sort fields' values: Count and totals summed, and a field whose values differ left empty. Each one given replaces the last; `fields: []` goes back to its category's

commands.label: Section
commands.parameters: {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

commands.label: Section Box
commands.parameters: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again

commands.label: Select by ID
commands.parameters: {text} the elements a list names, each by its id, its GUID (dashes and braces or not) or its IFC GlobalId, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or lines: `ids` found, each once in the order named, `missing` (what named none), and `plan` and `extent` ([[x, y], [x, y]] mm), the level's plan that shows them and where; it selects nothing itself, a front end does

commands.label: Shaft Opening
commands.parameters: {boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`

commands.label: Shared Parameters
commands.parameters: {path, action?: list|create|add_group|add|load|export, group?, name?, guid?, kind?: length|number|integer|angle|area|volume|yesno|material|text|url|familytype, of?: category, description?, visible?, modifiable?, family?, instance?, under?: constraints|construction|dimensions|graphics|identity-data|materials-and-finishes|text|visibility|electrical|mechanical|plumbing|structural|data|other, replace?} a shared parameters file, as Revit's Manage > Shared Parameters keeps one: a plain-text file of the user's own at `path` (given on every call; it is never part of the project), in Revit's tab-separated layout (versions 2 and 1 read, 2 written), listing groups and in them parameters, each a GUID, a name, a data type, a description, whether it is `visible` and whether the user may change it (`modifiable`). `list` (the default) reads it: its `version`, its groups (`id`, `name`) and each one's `parameters` (`guid`, `name`, `kind` — null for a data type BIMCraft has no kind for, which is listed and kept but can't be loaded — `datatype` as written, `of` for a family type, `description`, `visible`, `modifiable`, the `line` it is on, and the project's `families` holding it). `create` writes an empty file (refused over one there unless `replace`). `add_group` adds a `group`, named. `add` adds parameter `name` of `kind` to an existing `group`, with a new GUID unless `guid` is given, a family type with `of`, `description` one line, `visible` and `modifiable` true unless false. `load` adds a parameter of the file, by `name` or `guid`, to `family`, as Revit's Add Parameter > Shared Parameter does: its GUID becomes the parameter's `shared`, its name and kind are the file's (and can't be changed in the family), `instance` and `under` (the heading it is listed under; none, its kind's) are the caller's, and a family type whose category the file can't say takes `of`; refused where the family has a parameter of that name, or the project shares that GUID under another name or kind, or that name as another GUID. `export` writes `family`'s shared parameters (none named, every family's) into the file, creating it if there is none, new ones under `group` (by default the family's name, else `Exported Parameters`): what the file has by that GUID is kept as the file says it, and one the file holds as another name or kind, or a name it holds as another GUID, is refused naming its line. A file that isn't one is refused naming its line, and is never written over; files are capped at 4 MiB and 100,000 lines. Only `load` changes the project, one undo step

commands.label: Sheet
commands.parameters: {number?, name?, size?: ISO A0–A4|ISO B1–B4|ARCH A–E|ARCH E1–E3|ANSI A–E|SUPER B|width x height in mm, title_block?, fields?: {KEY: text}} a sheet of paper (A3 by default), with a title block: the built-in one, or the project's `title_block` of that name (see `title_block`), its sheet fields filled in from `fields`, or with `title_block` "none" (or false) none at all: no border, title box or folding marks, for one drawn on the sheet itself; named sizes landscape, custom ones as given, 100 to 1219.2 mm a side and, with a title block, wide enough for the standard's title block and margins (210 mm, 211.75 under ANSI); numbers run A101, A102…. `modify` changes them later: `title_block` ("" or true for the built-in, "none" or false for none), `fields` (a key's value null to clear it)

commands.label: Show Mass
commands.parameters: {view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's

commands.label: Sketch
commands.parameters: {lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about (numbered from 0): ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line too: a polyline round a bow tie crosses itself), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc, a circle or a curve is cut into chords, a circle into up to 8,193): past 200,000 of them, or when they lie so close together that telling which cross takes more than six million steps, it is refused at once. `sketch` on floor, ceiling, roof and shaft, and edit_boundary, take the same lines for one outline and its holes

commands.label: Specify Coordinates at a Point
commands.parameters: {at: [x,y,z] | [x,y], on?, level?, east, north, elevation, angle?} sets the active site so that internal point `at` has the shared coordinates given (mm), turned to `angle` (degrees from project north to true north, east positive) when given. A point picked in plan, `at: [x, y]`, takes its height from `on`, the element picked: a wall's bottom, a floor's, roof's or ceiling's top there; else from `level` (the lowest by default): the top of what stands on it there, else the level

commands.label: Split
commands.parameters: {id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`

commands.label: Spot Elevation
commands.parameters: {at: [x, y], view?, host?, origin?: base|survey} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up. It reads from `origin`: the Project Base Point (the default) or the Survey Point, the shared elevation

commands.label: Spot Coordinate
commands.parameters: {at: [x, y], view?, type?, origin?: base|survey|internal, host?, end?: [x, y], leader?, shoulder?} a spot coordinate in a level's plan (the lowest by default): the north and east of `at`, and its elevation, as its type (`spot_coordinate_type`) says. Without `type`, the project's type that reads from `origin`: the Survey Point (the shared coordinates of the active location, in metres) by default; `base`, the Project Base Point; `internal`. Its elevation is of the top of `host` (else of what stands at `at`, else of the level). Its leader runs from `at` to `end` (else up and to the right, 8 mm on paper), its text on a shoulder there; `leader: false` puts the text beside the point, `shoulder: false` leaves the shoulder out. `modify` changes `type`, `end`, `leader` and `shoulder`. The reply gives `north`, `east` (mm) and `text`, its lines

commands.label: Spot Coordinate Types
commands.parameters: {name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, …values} a spot coordinate type of the project's, as Revit's type parameters, lengths mm on paper. Constraints: `rotate_with_component` (its text turns with the component it reads). Graphics: `leader_arrowhead` filled|empty|dot|empty_dot|none, `arrowhead_size` (2.5), `leader_pen` and `arrowhead_pen` (0 to 16; 1), `leader_color` ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b]), `symbol` none|cross|target, `symbol_size` (3). Text: `font` (Arial), `text_size` (2.5), `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor` (1), `text_color`, `text_offset_leader` (1), `text_offset_symbol` (1), `text_location` above_leader|below_leader, `background` opaque|transparent, `origin` base|survey|internal (Coordinate Origin), `top` and `bottom` north_south|east_west|none (Top Value, Bottom Value), `north_south_indicator` ("N "), `east_west_indicator` ("E "), `include_elevation`, `elevation_indicator` ("EL "), `indicator` prefix|suffix, `units` (mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in; null for the project's) and `decimals` (0 to 6), `alternate` none|right|below with `alternate_units`, `alternate_decimals`, `alternate_prefix` and `alternate_suffix`. A new one starts as `like` says, else as the default. A project starts with `Spot Coordinate - Project Base Point` and `Spot Coordinate - Survey Point`. `rename` renames it, its spot coordinates following; `delete` takes it away while none is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

commands.label: Spot Slope
commands.parameters: {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot slope in a level's plan (the lowest by default): how steeply the top of the floor or roof at `at` (or `host`) falls there, %, an arrow pointing downhill; it follows the top. The reply gives `slope` and `toward`, the way down in plan (null on the level)

commands.label: Stair
commands.parameters: {start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too

commands.label: Technical Standards
commands.parameters: {set?: nbr|iso|ansi|eu|jis, adapt_all?: bool, adapt_line_weights?: bool, adapt_object_styles?: bool, adapt_units?: bool} configures the project's technical standard (NBR, ISO, ANSI, EU, JIS) and adapts line weights (pens), sheet layouts, object styles, and dimensioning conventions. NBR includes NBR 16861, NBR 16752, NBR 17006, NBR 17067, NBR 17068, and NBR 6492. The numbers each standard sets (margins, folds, pens, per-category pens) came with the contribution that added them and have not been checked against the standards named. Without `set`, reports the current standard and available standards

commands.label: Size a Storm Drain
commands.parameters: {kind: downpipe|horizontal, area?, rainfall?, flow?, outlet?: edge|funnel, gutter?, length?, slope?, inside?} a storm drain as NBR 10844 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/min), or the rain on `area` (m², as the standard counts a roof) at `rainfall` (mm/h; 150 by default, which the standard allows for up to 100 m² only: above that `rainfall` is required): Q = I·A/60. A `downpipe` (condutor vertical) takes the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses by Q, the water depth in the gutter `gutter` (50 to 100 mm), its `length` (mm, 0.3 m or more) and the gutter's `outlet` (edge: sharp-edged, the default; funnel); 70 mm inside at least. A `horizontal` drain takes Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, PVC only, from the standard's Table 2) at its `slope` (a fraction, 0.005 at least): the inner diameter it needs, and with `inside` (mm) whether that pipe carries the flow. Off the abacuses (more than 150 mm inside) nothing is read. A key that does not apply to the `kind`, or `flow` together with `area`, is an error. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
