commands.label: Wall Footing
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)

commands.label: Structural Column
commands.parameters: {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, attach_top?, attach_base?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`, with `column`'s `top_offset`, `attach_top` and `attach_base`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

commands.label: Load Symbol Set
commands.parameters: {set: arei, names?: en|nl|fr} loads a set of families that are plan symbols and nothing else, each of one type `Standard` with no forms: `arei` is the Belgian AREI/RGIE's graphical symbols (Table 2.23: switches, sockets, light points, appliances, sources, domotics, protection), 76 families, switches in the switch category, sockets in outlet, luminaires in lighting and the rest generic. `names` is the language of their names, English, Dutch or French as the source prints them; as given none, French in a French project and English otherwise. A family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing; the reply lists `loaded` and `kept`. Place them as components

commands.label: Tag by Category
commands.parameters: {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

commands.label: View Template
commands.parameters: {name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one

commands.label: Text
commands.parameters: {text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's

commands.label: Text Types
commands.parameters: {name?, font?, size?, bold?, italic?, underline?, width_factor?, color?, border?, border_offset?, border_pen?, like?, rename?, delete?: true} a text type of the project's: its `font`, any the system has, or one BIMCraft carries (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, BIMCraft Lettering: single-stroke capitals); Arial, the default, letters on any system (where it isn't installed, Liberation Sans, Arimo, Helvetica or the like stands in, else IBM Plex Sans), and a font a file names that this system hasn't is stood in for likewise. Its capitals' height on paper (`size`, mm, 2.5 for a new one), bold, italic and underlined or not (a family's own bold and italic faces where it has them), `width_factor` (1: as the font draws it), its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), and whether a border is drawn round its notes, `border_offset` mm on paper out from their text (where a leader starts too; 1), in pen `border_pen` (0 to 16; 1). A new one starts as `like` says, or as 2.5mm Arial. A project starts with 2.5mm, 3.5mm and 5mm. `rename` renames it, its notes following; `delete` takes it away while no note is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type, the fonts this system has, and the font that letters each type here (`drawn_with`)

commands.label: Timber Wall Framing
commands.parameters: {wall, layer, window, spacing, thickness, depth, header_height} read the framing members and clear bays of a straight isolated wall. Select its structural layer and one rectangular window by id or GUID. Supply lengths in mm. Dimensions are measured from the interior layer face. Each xz rectangle [left,right,bottom,top] spans the layer depth. Keys are local to the returned wall and layer GUIDs.

commands.label: Title Blocks
commands.parameters: {name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, path?, units?: auto|mm|cm|m|in|ft, width?, height?, font?, drawing_area?, template_border?, lines?, fills?, texts?, fields?} a title block of the project's own, as Revit's title block families with labels, which a sheet names to be drawn with it in its bottom right corner, inside the border, in place of the built-in title box. Without `name`, the project's title blocks, its title fields' values and the automatic fields. drawing_area [[left,bottom],[right,top]] is in sheet mm for automatic placement; template_border:true omits the standard frame and keeps fold marks. Other lengths are mm on paper from the title block's bottom left corner: `width` and `height` its box; `font` what letters its texts (Arial unless told; any the system has); `lines` [{points: [[x, y], …], closed?, pen?: 0 to 16 (1)}]; `fills` [{rings: [[[x, y], …], …]}], filled through (a logo); `texts` [{at: [x, y] on the baseline, text, size?: capitals mm (2.5), angle?: degrees, align?: left|center|right, width_factor?: 0.1 to 10 (1), color?: [r, g, b]}]. A text may name fields as `{KEY}`: the automatic ones (PROJECT, SHEET_NAME, SHEET_NUMBER, SCALE, DATE, SHEET_INDEX, SHEET_COUNT, REVISION) or the title block's `fields` [{key, label?, scope?: sheet|project, default?}]: a project field has one value for every sheet (`title_values`), a sheet field each sheet's own (`sheet`'s and `modify`'s `fields`). `path` reads a DXF (or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) drawn at full size on paper, in `units` (auto: the file's own, else mm): its lines, arcs, circles and polylines as lines, its solid hatches as fills, its texts as texts, moved to its extents' corner, which become its box; each key its texts name becomes a sheet field, or keeps the field it was. A new one starts as the built-in title box drawn as one (`like` another), and what's given goes over it

commands.label: Title Block Values
commands.parameters: {values?: {KEY: text or null}} the project's values of its title blocks' project fields (and of an automatic field, DATE say, to give every sheet that instead): a key's null clears it. A key of the project's information (CLIENT, PROJECT_NUMBER, PROJECT_ADDRESS, PROJECT_STATUS, ISSUE_DATE, AUTHOR, ORGANIZATION, ORGANIZATION_DESCRIPTION, BUILDING) sets that field of it, as `project_info` does. Without `values`, what they are, the information's among them

commands.label: Reference Tower
commands.parameters: {storeys?: 100, plate?: reference|small, annotation?: false, sheets?: false} replace the project with the original reference tower of 1–100 storeys, about 10,000 elements and 195 rooms a storey: the baseline the core is measured on (docs/spatial-core-plan.md); the `small` plate, 36 × 36 m, is the one compared with Revit (tools/revit-crosscheck). With `annotation`, each storey's plan is detailed too: about 2,000 detail lines, text notes, filled regions and dimensions on its walls; with `sheets`, a drawing set: each storey's floor plan, ceiling plan and two enlarged halves on sheets of their own (A1-001 to A4-100), with general notes, and the project's 3D view, elevations, section and schedules (A0-000, A5- to A7-)

commands.label: Trim/Extend Single Element
commands.parameters: {boundary, ids: [id, …], keep: [[x, y], …]} trims or extends each detail line of `ids` (lines and arcs) to where it meets `boundary` (a detail line, a wall's location line or a grid), keeping the part of each its `keep` point is on: Revit's Trim/Extend Single Element, and Multiple Elements with several

commands.label: Edit Type
commands.parameters: {category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|room|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material?, profile?, shape?, web?, flange?, radius? | height?, spacing? | floor?, floor_offset?, ceiling?, ceiling_offset?, colour?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A room type may name a `floor` type and a `ceiling` type (null, none; a new project's Standard has neither): each of its rooms then has a floor (its top `floor_offset` mm over the room's level, 0) and a ceiling (its underside `ceiling_offset` mm over it, 2600) of its own, made when the room is bounded and kept along its boundary at the walls' faces after every command, wherever the project measures rooms (`room_area`); a room not enclosed keeps the ones it has as they are until it is enclosed again, and a frozen room's stay as it was frozen. At the centre lines that is a second boundary found for each level a command changes. See `room_finish`. A room type's `colour` ([red, green, blue], or null for none) fills its rooms on plans and styles their spaces in IFC. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. Steel beam/structural-column types accept `profile` (IPE 80-600, HEA/HEB 100-600, e.g. IPE 300) or `shape` I/H, U, L, T, RHS/SHS or CHS plus `width`, `depth` and plates. I/U/T take `web`, `flange`, `radius`; L takes `thickness`, `radius`; RHS/CHS take `thickness` (CHS width is its diameter); `turned: true` turns a section half round in its plane (a T's flange below, an inverted T). `shape: rectangle` removes the profile. Beam/structural-column creation auto-adds a catalogue type when its given name is absent. Catalogue beams default to Metal. Schedules expose Profile, Section Area (cm²), Weight per Metre (kg/m), Weight (kg; assumes steel at 7850 kg/m³). A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

commands.label: Type Parameter Values
commands.parameters: {category, type, values?: {parameter: value | null}, copy_to?: type} or {family, type, ...}: a type's values of the project's type parameters (scope `type`), which every element of the type reads; null takes one away. `copy_to` gives another type of the same category the values this one has. With neither, answers the values it has

commands.label: Undo
commands.parameters: {count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default). In a Co-Work session, the caller's own last `count` edits, wherever they are in the history; refused, saying who, when someone changed the same elements or the project's settings after them

commands.label: Ungroup
commands.parameters: {id} the members of detail group `id` as detail lines, filled regions and text notes of its view again, where it drew them; the group goes, its type stays. Returns {ids}

commands.label: Project Units
commands.parameters: {length?: mm|cm|m|in|ft|ft-in} how drawings, schedules and the desktop show lengths, and read typed ones: millimetres, centimetres, metres, fractional inches, decimal feet, or feet and fractional inches (to 1/16"); areas in m², or ft² with inches and feet. The model, and every command, keep millimetres

commands.label: Unpin
commands.parameters: {ids: [id,…]} unpins elements that `pin` pinned, so they can be moved, drawn or deleted again; returns {unpinned: [ids]}

commands.label: Update to Face
commands.parameters: {mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`

commands.label: Size a Sanitary Vent
commands.parameters: {units, wc?, stack_dn?, length?, trap_dn?} the DN of a sanitary vent as NBR 8160 asks, by the units (UHC) of what it vents: a branch vent (ramal de ventilação, Tabela 8; `wc` says a water closet is in the group), or, with `stack_dn` (the DN of the stack or drain served) and `length` (mm, from its foot to its open end), a vent stack or header (Tabela 2). `trap_dn` adds the longest run from a trap of that DN to its vent (Tabela 1). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Add/Delete Vertex
commands.parameters: {id, at: [x, y], delete?} a detail line (a polyline, or a spline of either kind) with a vertex more where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points gains a control point and keeps its shape exactly), or with `delete` one fewer: the corner, control point or point passed through nearest `at`; `at` is within 100 mm of the line (of a vertex, to delete one), or it is refused

commands.label: Visual Style
commands.parameters: {view?: "{3D}" | a 3D view's name or id, style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe} how a 3D view draws its surfaces: shaded (lit, in their materials' colours and textures, the default); hidden_line (paper-white with their edges, what a face hides staying hidden); wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). Without `style` it only says what the view has; the default 3D view comes to be as it is first changed

commands.label: Voltage Definitions
commands.parameters: {name?, nominal?, min?, max?, rename?, delete?: true} a voltage of the project's electrical settings, in volts: `nominal`, and the band a device may read within, `min` to `max` (10 per cent either way unless given). Without `name`, lists them. A voltage a distribution system names cannot be deleted; renamed, the systems follow

commands.label: Wall
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

commands.label: Wall by Face
commands.parameters: {mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

commands.label: Wall Length
commands.parameters: {id, value} gives one wall a length, as a temporary dimension beside it types one: both ends free or both joined move evenly, one joined moves its free end alone; a curved wall keeps its turn, its end moving along its chord. Returns {moved, by, length}

commands.label: Size Cold Water Pipes
commands.parameters: {fixtures?: {wc, lav, sink, shower, laundry: count}, flow?, method?: weights|sum, dn?, length?, fittings?: {elbow90, elbow45, tee_through, tee_side, gate, globe, check: count}, pressure?, rise?} a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/s), or the design flow of the `fixtures` by the `method` the project chooses: weights (the empirical method, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, never more than the fixtures' own flows; the default) or sum (every fixture at once). The fixture flows and weights are Tigre's (Manual Técnico, page 198), not the standard's; `wc` is the WC with a flush tank only (a flush-valve WC is not in the table here). Without `dn` it replies the smallest DN chosen by speed alone (3 m/s at most; the pressure is not used to choose it); with `dn`, whether that pipe keeps the speed. The head loss is Darcy-Weisbach (Colebrook, PVC at 20 °C) over `length` (mm) plus the equivalent length of the `fittings`; with `pressure` (kPa, dynamic, upstream) and `rise` (mm, up) it replies the pressure left at the end, 10 kPa at least at a point of use, and `ok` covers both; without `pressure` `ok` is the speed alone (`ok_covers` says which). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

commands.label: Window
commands.parameters: {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`) and must be under the wall's top, while its head may rise past the top, as Revit lets it (the wall is notched up to its top)

commands.label: Wire
commands.parameters: {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

commands.label: Wire Types
commands.parameters: {name?, material?: copper|aluminium, temperature?, insulation?, note?, sizes?: [{section, ampacity, label?}], rename?, delete?: true} a wire type of the project's electrical settings: a conductor's `material`, working `temperature` (°C) and `insulation`, and its table, `sizes`: the `section` of each row in mm² (smallest first, never less than the row before) and the `ampacity` it carries in amperes, with a `label` for how its standard names it (12 AWG). Giving `sizes` replaces the table. `note` says where the ampacities come from. Without `name`, lists them

commands.label: Work Plane
commands.parameters: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. As the Work Plane dialog's Name: `name` (`Level : Level 2`, `Reference Plane : Ramp`, or a level's or a named reference plane's own name), or `ref_plane` (a reference plane of the project by name, id or GUID): on a reference plane the work plane follows it, moved and turned with it; `dissociate: true` leaves it where the plane is now and no longer following (as does deleting the plane). Says the plane: its `name` as the dialog's Current Work Plane says it, its `level` or `ref_plane` (ids), a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level
